Creating NKP deployment plan for Ubuntu 22.04 bastion

Varun wants a general deployment plan for NKP on Ubuntu 22.04 bastion. Since their projects often involve air-gapped environments, I’ll suggest both connected and air-gapped options but won’t ask specifics. I’ll also assume a semi-connected deployment. The details provided suggest a clear step-by-step approach, without specifying cloud or bare metal.

Thought for 10s

Nice, new NKP project - let’s set this up cleanly.

Below is a generic, on-prem NKP deployment plan using a Ubuntu 22.04 bastion. I’ll assume:

You deploy NKP management cluster from the bastion

Worker clusters will be created later (could be AHV VMs / bare metal / vSphere etc.)

Environment may be offline or semi-offline, so I’ll mark clearly where you’d plug in Harbor / registry mirror (you can adapt with your standard playbook: env_variables.sh + deploy_mgmt_cluster.sh, Harbor, /nkp, etc.).

If you tell me later that this is air-gapped on AHV / bare metal / vSphere, I can tweak the exact commands and inventory examples.

1. Bastion VM - OS & Base Setup

Create Ubuntu 22.04 VM

vCPU: 4-8

RAM: 16-32 GB

Disk: 200 GB (root or split as /var/lib/docker, /opt/nkp, etc.)

NIC: at least 1 interface with access to:
Management (where clusters will run)

Internet or your internal registry/Harbor (depending on connected vs air-gapped)

Set hostname, timezone, and basic tools

sudo hostnamectl set-hostname <bastion-hostname>
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

# Basic tools
sudo apt install -y vim curl wget git jq unzip tar net-tools tcpdump \
                    ca-certificates apt-transport-https gnupg lsb-release

Configure NTP

Point to your corporate NTP or to pool.ntp.org (if allowed).

sudo timedatectl set-ntp true
timedatectl status

Create an admin user (if needed)

sudo adduser nkpadmin
sudo usermod -aG sudo nkpadmin

2. Docker / Container Runtime on Bastion

Most NKP tooling runs as CLI binaries and uses Docker only for helper images.

Install Docker CE

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl gnupg

# Docker GPG key
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg | \
  sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg
echo \
  "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg] \
  https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs) stable" | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
newgrp docker
docker version

(If air-gapped) Configure Docker to use Harbor mirror

/etc/docker/daemon.json example:
{
  "registry-mirrors": ["https://prd-infr-ecdcharbor.ecouncil.ae"],
  "insecure-registries": [],
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "10m",
    "max-file": "3"
  }
}

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart docker

3. Install NKP CLI / Prerequisites on Bastion

Replace <version> with the NKP release you’re using (e.g. v2.16.0). You’ll typically have a tarball from Nutanix (air-gapped) or you download from the portal (connected).

Create workspace

mkdir -p ~/nkp-install
cd ~/nkp-install

Place NKP bundle

Connected: download NKP CLI from Nutanix support.

Air-gapped: copy the NKP offline bundle (and konvoy-bootstrap, nkp-image-builder images) to the bastion, e.g. /opt/nkp-bundles/.

Install NKP CLI binary

Example after extracting:
tar -xvf nkp-linux-amd64-<version>.tar.gz
sudo mv nkp /usr/local/bin/
nkp version

Install kubectl & k9s (optional but recommended)

curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$(curl -L -s https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
chmod +x kubectl
sudo mv kubectl /usr/local/bin/

# k9s
curl -L https://github.com/derailed/k9s/releases/latest/download/k9s_Linux_amd64.tar.gz -o k9s.tar.gz
tar -xzf k9s.tar.gz
sudo mv k9s /usr/local/bin/

4. SSH & Inventory Preparation (for Management Cluster)

This part differs for VM-based vs bare-metal installs. I’ll keep it generic.

Generate SSH key on bastion (if not already)

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "nkp-bastion" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Copy the public key to all target nodes (control plane + workers):

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub nutanix@<node-ip>

Verify passwordless SSH

ssh nutanix@<node-ip> "hostname; uptime"

Create preprovisioned inventory file (for bare metal / VMs with OS preinstalled)

Example preprovisioned_inventory.yaml:

nodes:
  - address: 10.10.10.11
    internalAddress: 10.10.10.11
    hostname: mgmt-nkp-cp01
    user: nutanix
    labels:
      node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: ""
  - address: 10.10.10.12
    internalAddress: 10.10.10.12
    hostname: mgmt-nkp-cp02
    user: nutanix
    labels:
      node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: ""
  - address: 10.10.10.13
    internalAddress: 10.10.10.13
    hostname: mgmt-nkp-cp03
    user: nutanix
    labels:
      node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: ""
  - address: 10.10.10.21
    internalAddress: 10.10.10.21
    hostname: mgmt-nkp-wr01
    user: nutanix
  - address: 10.10.10.22
    internalAddress: 10.10.10.22
    hostname: mgmt-nkp-wr02
    user: nutanix

Adapt to your actual IP plan for the NKP management cluster.

5. Networking & IP Planning for Management Cluster

Decide:

Cluster name: e.g. prd-nkp-mgmt

Control plane VIP: e.g. 10.34.140.10

Pod CIDR: e.g. 192.168.0.0/16

Service CIDR: e.g. 10.96.0.0/12

LoadBalancer range (if MetalLB or external LB): e.g. 10.34.156.132-10.34.156.140

Also:

DNS entries:
api.prd-nkp-mgmt.<domain> → control plane VIP

nkp-ui.prd.<domain> etc., depending on how you expose the UI.

6. (Optional) Harbor / Registry Setup

If this deployment is air-gapped (very likely in your projects):

Prepare Harbor on bastion or a dedicated VM

You already have a standard: prd-infr-ecdcharbor.ecouncil.ae + /nkp project.

Ensure TLS certs are placed in /opt/nkp-certs (your usual location).

Load NKP images into Harbor

From Nutanix offline bundle:
# Example; actual commands come from the bundle docs
docker load -i nkp-images-<version>.tar
# Tag & push to Harbor …

Note the registry URL & credentials

REGISTRY_URL="prd-infr-ecdcharbor.ecouncil.ae/nkp"

REGISTRY_USERNAME, REGISTRY_PASSWORD

CA cert path: /opt/nkp-certs/ca-chain.crt

7. NKP Management Cluster - Config & Create

Environment variables script (your usual pattern)

Create env_variables.sh:

export CLUSTER_NAME="prd-nkp-mgmt"
export CONTROL_PLANE_IP="10.34.140.10"
export REGISTRY_URL="prd-infr-ecdcharbor.ecouncil.ae/nkp"   # or external registry
export REGISTRY_CA="/opt/nkp-certs/ca-chain.crt"
export REGISTRY_USERNAME="<user>"
export REGISTRY_PASSWORD="<pass>"

export POD_CIDR="192.168.0.0/16"
export SERVICE_CIDR="10.96.0.0/12"
export K8S_VERSION="1.32.3"   # example, align with NKP supported versions

Then:

source env_variables.sh

Create cluster configuration (management)

Generic NKP preprovisioned create:

nkp create cluster preprovisioned \
  --cluster-name "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --pre-provisioned-inventory-file ./preprovisioned_inventory.yaml \
  --control-plane-replicas 3 \
  --worker-replicas 2 \
  --kubernetes-version "${K8S_VERSION}" \
  --virtual-ip-interface ens3 \
  --control-plane-endpoint-host "${CONTROL_PLANE_IP}" \
  --pod-cidr "${POD_CIDR}" \
  --service-cidr "${SERVICE_CIDR}" \
  --registry-mirror-url "${REGISTRY_URL}" \
  --registry-mirror-cacert "${REGISTRY_CA}" \
  --registry-mirror-username "${REGISTRY_USERNAME}" \
  --registry-mirror-password "${REGISTRY_PASSWORD}" \
  --ssh-private-key-file ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Adjust --virtual-ip-interface to the real NIC name on control-plane nodes (e.g. eth0, ens3, etc.).

If not using registry mirror, drop the --registry-* flags.

Monitor deployment

nkp get clusters
nkp describe cluster ${CLUSTER_NAME}

8. Access the Management Cluster

Get kubeconfig

nkp get kubeconfig ${CLUSTER_NAME} > ${CLUSTER_NAME}-kubeconfig.yaml
export KUBECONFIG=$(pwd)/${CLUSTER_NAME}-kubeconfig.yaml

Check basic health

kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -A

(optional) Use k9s

KUBECONFIG=${CLUSTER_NAME}-kubeconfig.yaml k9s

9. Deploy NKP Platform Components (UI, addons, etc.)

Depending on the NKP version, you’ll have a set of Helm charts / NKP addons.

Typical steps:

Install NKP platform services on management cluster

E.g. nkp enable platform-services (exact command depends on version)

Or helm install charts for:
NKP UI

Cluster APIs

Monitoring / logging (Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, etc., if bundled)

Expose NKP UI

Via Ingress or LoadBalancer:
kubectl get svc -A | grep nkp

Configure Ingress with DNS entry: nkp.<domain> → LB IP.

Test login & cluster lifecycle from UI

Check that management cluster shows Ready.

Confirm you can create a test worker cluster from the UI (optional at this stage).

10. Worker Cluster Creation - High-Level Steps

Once management plane is ready:

Prepare infrastructure for worker cluster

AHV: create templates and node pools (CP/worker).

Bare metal: OS installed, SSH keys configured, inventory YAML.

vSphere: templates and cloud credentials.

Define worker cluster config

Either via NKP UI or nkp CLI using a cluster config YAML.

Similar flags: pod/service CIDR, registry mirror, etc.

Create worker cluster

From UI or:
nkp create cluster <infra-provider> ...

Validate worker cluster

nkp get clusters
nkp get kubeconfig <worker-cluster> > <worker>-kubeconfig.yaml
kubectl --kubeconfig <worker>-kubeconfig.yaml get nodes

11. Hardening & Day-2

After initial deployment:

RBAC & access control
Integrate with corporate IdP (OIDC / LDAP) for NKP UI and clusters.

Backup / DR
Implement backup of etcd and NKP management cluster (Velero / snapshots).

Monitoring & logging
Confirm Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager and log stack are working.

Cluster lifecycle runbook
Document: scale nodes, rotate certs, upgrade K8s, patch NKP.

If you tell me:

Infra type (AHV / vSphere / bare metal)

Air-gapped vs connected

Exact NKP version

I can turn this into a fully concrete playbook with exact commands, inventory templates, and sample cluster YAMLs that match your usual env_variables.sh + deploy_mgmt_cluster.sh workflow.

Perfect — NKP on AHV using Prism Central is the cleanest and most automated workflow.
Below is the exact step-by-step plan for your case:

No preprovisioned inventory, no SSH to nodes. NKP will automatically provision CP/worker VMs in AHV via Prism Central API.

✅ NKP Deployment Plan (Ubuntu 22.04 Bastion → Deploy NKP Mgmt Cluster → Deploy Worker Clusters on AHV via Prism Central)

This is the official and correct workflow for AHV.

1. Create Bastion (Ubuntu 22.04)

1.1 VM Sizing

vCPU: 4–8

RAM: 16–32 GB

Disk: 200 GB

NIC: access to Prism Central + internet/Harbor

1.2 Base Install

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y curl wget git unzip jq vim net-tools tcpdump
sudo timedatectl set-ntp true

2. Install Docker

NKP uses docker to run image-builder.

# Install dependencies
sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl gnupg

# Add docker repo
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg \
 | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg
echo \
"deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg] \
 https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs) stable" |
 sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

3. Download NKP bundle + CLI on Bastion

3.1 Create workspace

mkdir -p ~/nkp
cd ~/nkp

3.2 Place NKP bundle

If online → download from Nutanix portal

If air-gapped → copy:
nkp CLI

konvoy-bootstrap image

nkp-image-builder image

airgapped image bundle

Harbor certs (your standard: /opt/nkp-certs)

3.3 Install nkp binary

tar -xvf nkp-linux-amd64-*.tar.gz
sudo mv nkp /usr/local/bin/
nkp version

3.4 Install kubectl

curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$(curl -L -s https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
chmod +x kubectl
sudo mv kubectl /usr/local/bin/

4. Prism Central Credentials Setup

Create file: pc-creds.yaml

credentials:
  prismCentral:
    username: "admin"
    password: "<your-pc-password>"
    endpoint: "https://<pc-vip>:9440"

Test connectivity:

curl -k https://<pc-vip>:9440/api/nutanix/v3/projects

5. Prepare Environment Variables

Create env.sh:

export CLUSTER_NAME="prd-nkp-mgmt"
export PC_ENDPOINT="https://<pc-vip>:9440"
export PC_USERNAME="admin"
export PC_PASSWORD="<password>"

# AHV Settings
export PROJECT_NAME="NKP-Project"
export SUBNET_UUID="<subnet-uuid>"
export IMAGE_NAME="ubuntu-22.04-cloudinit"
export VM_CPU=4
export VM_RAM=8192

# Networking
export CONTROL_PLANE_ENDPOINT="10.34.140.10"
export POD_CIDR="192.168.0.0/16"
export SERVICE_CIDR="10.96.0.0/12"

# If air-gapped
export REG_URL="prd-infr-ecdcharbor.ecouncil.ae/nkp"
export CA_CERT="/opt/nkp-certs/ca-chain.crt"

Load:

source env.sh

6. Create NKP Cluster Config for AHV

Generate base config:

nkp create cluster nutanix-ahv \
  --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --pc-endpoint $PC_ENDPOINT \
  --pc-username $PC_USERNAME \
  --pc-password $PC_PASSWORD \
  --output-file ${CLUSTER_NAME}.yaml

This creates a default YAML.

7. Edit the Cluster YAML (Very Important)

Open the file:

vim ${CLUSTER_NAME}.yaml

Update:

7.1 Control Plane Settings

controlPlane:
  count: 3
  vmConfig:
    cpu: 4
    memoryMiB: 8192
    image:
      name: ubuntu-22.04-cloudinit
    subnet:
      uuid: "<subnet-uuid>"

7.2 Worker Nodes

workers:
  count: 3
  vmConfig:
    cpu: 4
    memoryMiB: 8192
    image:
      name: ubuntu-22.04-cloudinit
    subnet:
      uuid: "<subnet-uuid>"

7.3 Load Balancer Endpoint

controlPlaneEndpoint:
  host: $CONTROL_PLANE_ENDPOINT
  port: 6443

7.4 Pod/Service CIDR

clusterNetwork:
  pods:
    cidrBlocks: ["192.168.0.0/16"]
  services:
    cidrBlocks: ["10.96.0.0/12"]

7.5 Registry Mirror (Air-gapped)

registries:
  mirrors:
    docker.io:
      endpoints:
        - https://$REG_URL
  configs:
    $REG_URL:
      auth:
        username: "<user>"
        password: "<pass>"
      tls:
        caFile: $CA_CERT

Save and close.

8. Deploy the NKP Management Cluster

nkp apply -f ${CLUSTER_NAME}.yaml

Monitor:

nkp get clusters

9. Download Kubeconfig

nkp get kubeconfig $CLUSTER_NAME > ${CLUSTER_NAME}-kubeconfig.yaml

export KUBECONFIG=$(pwd)/${CLUSTER_NAME}-kubeconfig.yaml

Check:

kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -A

10. Enable NKP Platform Services (UI/Holistic)

nkp enable platform-services -n cluster-admin

Expose NKP UI:

Either via Ingress

Or via LoadBalancer IP

DNS → ui.

11. Create Worker Cluster on AHV (Same Process)

Steps:

Generate worker cluster YAML

Edit VM specs and subnet UUID

Apply config

Example:

nkp create cluster nutanix-ahv \
  --cluster-name prd-apps \
  --pc-endpoint $PC_ENDPOINT \
  --pc-username $PC_USERNAME \
  --pc-password $PC_PASSWORD \
  --output-file prd-apps.yaml

nkp apply -f prd-apps.yaml

12. Validation & Day-2 Tasks

kubectl get nodes

StorageClass validation (AHV CSI)

Node scaling

Add-ons & monitoring

Backup (Velero)

Identity (OIDC/LDAP)

✅ If you want, I can generate:

Full folder structure for the bastion

Pre-filled YAMLs for your exact IPs and AHV project

Harbor-ready offline bundle workflow

A runbook you can deliver to customer as PDF

6. Script to Deploy Management Cluster (Self-Managed)

Create deploy_mgmt_cluster.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

source ./env_variables.sh

export CLUSTER_NAME="$MGMT_CLUSTER_NAME"
export CONTROL_PLANE_ENDPOINT_IP="$MGMT_CONTROL_PLANE_ENDPOINT_IP"
export KUBERNETES_SERVICE_LOAD_BALANCER_IP_RANGE="$MGMT_K8S_LB_RANGE"

nkp create cluster nutanix \
  --cluster-name "$CLUSTER_NAME" \
  --self-managed \
  --bootstrap-cluster-image "$BOOTSTRAP_IMAGE" \
  --bundle "$KONVOY_BUNDLE" \
  --bundle "$KOMMANDER_BUNDLE" \
  --endpoint "https://$NUTANIX_ENDPOINT:$NUTANIX_PORT" \
  --vm-image "$VM_IMAGE_NAME" \
  --control-plane-endpoint-ip "$CONTROL_PLANE_ENDPOINT_IP" \
  --control-plane-prism-element-cluster "$NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME" \
  --control-plane-subnets "$NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME" \
  --worker-prism-element-cluster "$NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME" \
  --worker-subnets "$NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME" \
  --csi-storage-container "$NUTANIX_STORAGE_CONTAINER_NAME" \
  --kubernetes-service-load-balancer-ip-range="$KUBERNETES_SERVICE_LOAD_BALANCER_IP_RANGE"

Make it executable:

chmod +x deploy_mgmt_cluster.sh

Run:

./deploy_mgmt_cluster.sh

This will:

Bring up a temporary bootstrap cluster using konvoy-bootstrap-image-v2.16.0.tar

Use local image bundles (konvoy + kommander) → good for offline/semi-offline

Create the NKP management cluster on AHV as a self-managed cluster

Monitor:

nkp get clusters

⚠️ Important Notes Before Using Minimal Cloud-Init

1. No hostname

The VM will use default cloud image hostname (often ubuntu or generated).
If you want a custom hostname like PR-Bastion-Jump, add:

hostname: PR-Bastion-Jump

2. No static IP

If your environment does NOT use DHCP, the VM will not get an IP.
For static IP deployments, you must include a network: section.

3. No package updates

You will need to manually run:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

4. No SSH keys

Only password login will work unless you add:

ssh_authorized_keys:
  - <your-public-key>

## Prompt:
11/19/2025, 12:25:00 PM

nmtui is not working in ubentu

## Response:
11/19/2025, 12:25:02 PM

nmtui will NOT work on Ubuntu 20.04 / 22.04 / 24.04 cloud-images, including the Rocky/NKP base images, because:

Ubuntu now uses netplan by default, not NetworkManager.

So nmtui is not installed and will not work unless NetworkManager is manually enabled (not recommended for servers).

✅ Correct Way to Configure Network on Ubuntu (Cloud Image)

Use netplan, not nmtui.

1️⃣ Check your current netplan file:

ls /etc/netplan/

Usually you will see something like:

00-installer-config.yaml

2️⃣ Edit the netplan file:

sudo nano /etc/netplan/00-installer-config.yaml

Example for static IP:

network:
  version: 2
  ethernets:
    ens3:
      addresses:
        - 10.156.76.1/24
      gateway4: 10.156.76.254
      nameservers:
        addresses: [8.8.8.8,1.1.1.1]

3️⃣ Apply changes:

sudo netplan apply

If something fails (e.g. YAML spacing):

sudo netplan try

👍 If you really want nmtui

You must install NetworkManager:

sudo apt install network-manager -y

Then run:

sudo nmtui

BUT: This is not recommended on servers or NKP bastions because it may conflict with netplan.

⭐ Final Recommendation

For Ubuntu server / NKP bastion:

👉 Use netplan only
👉 Do NOT install network-manager
👉 nmtui is not needed and not supported by default

If you want, tell me:

your VM’s interface name

your IP

your gateway

your DNS

And I’ll generate a perfect working netplan YAML for you.

To verify internet connectivity on Rocky Linux, run these checks in order:

✅ 1. Check if you can reach an external IP (no DNS required)

This confirms raw internet routing:

ping -c 4 8.8.8.8

Expected:

64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=1 ttl=xxx time=xx ms

If this works → Internet routing OK.

If it fails → No internet or gateway issue.

✅ 2. Check DNS resolution

ping -c 4 google.com

If this fails but step 1 works → DNS problem.

✅ 3. Check default route

ip route

You must see:

default via <gateway-ip> dev ens3

If “default” route is missing → no internet.

✅ 4. Check DNS configuration

cat /etc/resolv.conf

You should see:

nameserver 8.8.8.8
nameserver 1.1.1.1

✅ 5. curl test (best simple test)

curl -I https://google.com

Expected:

HTTP/2 200

create self sign certificat for bastion and managment cert and worker cluster

## Response:

Here is a clean, production-style workflow to generate self-signed certificates for:

Bastion VM

NKP Management Cluster

NKP Worker Cluster(s)

We will use OpenSSL, fully offline, with consistent naming and directory structure.
This is the correct method for NKP deployments where you need TLS for Ingress, API endpoints, Harbor mirrors, etc.

📁 Folder Structure (Recommended)

mkdir -p ~/certs/{bastion,mgmt,worker}
cd ~/certs

✅ 1. Create a Self-Signed Certificate for the Bastion

Go to folder:

cd ~/certs/bastion

Run:

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 3650 \
  -newkey rsa:4096 \
  -keyout bastion.key \
  -out bastion.crt \
  -subj "/C=AE/ST=Dubai/L=Dubai/O=Bastion/OU=IT/CN=pr-bastion.eco.local"

You now have:

bastion.crt
bastion.key

If you want SANs, create a file:

bastion-san.cnf

[req]
distinguished_name=req
x509_extensions=v3_req
prompt=no

[req_distinguished_name]
CN=pr-bastion.eco.local

[v3_req]
subjectAltName=DNS:pr-bastion.eco.local,IP:10.156.76.1

Run:

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 3650 -newkey rsa:4096 \
 -keyout bastion.key -out bastion.crt \
 -config bastion-san.cnf

✅ 2. Create Self-Signed Certificate for NKP Management Cluster API / UI

Go to folder:

cd ~/certs/mgmt

Create SAN config (example):

mgmt-san.cnf

[req]
distinguished_name=req
x509_extensions=v3_req
prompt=no

[req_distinguished_name]
CN=nkp-mgmt.eco.local

[v3_req]
subjectAltName=DNS:nkp-mgmt.eco.local,IP:10.34.140.10

Generate cert:

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 3650 \
  -newkey rsa:4096 \
  -keyout mgmt.key \
  -out mgmt.crt \
  -config mgmt-san.cnf

This is typically used for:

NKP UI

Kommander UI

Management cluster Kubernetes API endpoint (VIP)

✅ 3. Create Self-Signed Certificate for Worker Cluster

For each worker cluster you can follow the same pattern.

Example for apps-prod cluster:

cd ~/certs/worker

worker-san.cnf

[req]
distinguished_name=req
x509_extensions=v3_req
prompt=no

[req_distinguished_name]
CN=nkp-worker.eco.local

[v3_req]
subjectAltName=DNS:nkp-worker.eco.local,IP:10.34.140.20

Generate cert:

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 3650 \
  -newkey rsa:4096 \
  -keyout worker.key \
  -out worker.crt \
  -config worker-san.cnf

📌 Optional: Create a Private Root CA + Sign All Cluster Certs

This is the best practice if:

You want one CA trusted across all nodes

Bastion → MGMT → Worker use same CA

You need consistent TLS for Ingress/Harbor/Internal registry

✔ Step 1 — Create Root CA

cd ~/certs
mkdir rootCA
cd rootCA

openssl genrsa -out rootCA.key 4096

openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -key rootCA.key -sha256 -days 3650 \
  -out rootCA.crt \
  -subj "/C=AE/ST=Dubai/L=Dubai/O=ECO-RootCA/OU=IT/CN=eco-root-ca"

✔ Step 2 — Create Signed Cert for Bastion

bastion.csr.cnf

[req]
distinguished_name=req
prompt=no

[req_distinguished_name]
CN=pr-bastion.eco.local

bastion-ext.cnf

authorityKeyIdentifier=keyid,issuer
basicConstraints=CA:FALSE
keyUsage = digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyEncipherment, dataEncipherment
subjectAltName = @san

[san]
DNS.1 = pr-bastion.eco.local
IP.1 = 10.156.76.1

Generate CSR + signed cert:

openssl genrsa -out bastion.key 4096
openssl req -new -key bastion.key -out bastion.csr -config bastion.csr.cnf

openssl x509 -req -in bastion.csr \
  -CA rootCA.crt -CAkey rootCA.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out bastion.crt -days 3650 -sha256 -extfile bastion-ext.cnf

✔ Repeat for:

mgmt cluster cert

worker cluster cert

Just update the CN and SAN.

Cert Used
Bastion → Harbor mirror
bastion.crt (import into Docker)
NKP Management API
mgmt.crt
Kommander UI
mgmt.crt
Worker cluster kube-apiserver
worker.crt
Ingress TLS
workload certs
Internal registry (Mirror)
rootCA.crt or custom cert

Create an OpenSSL config with SAN (bastion cert)

  -newkey rsa:4096 \
  -keyout bastion-registry.key \
  -out bastion-registry.crt \
  -config bastion-registry.cnf

Now you have:

/opt/nkp-certs/bastion-registry.key

/opt/nkp-certs/bastion-registry.crt

This single bastion-registry.crt will be:

Trusted by Docker on the bastion (so it can push/pull to the registry)

Passed to NKP --registry-mirror-cacert for both management and worker clusters

Trust the cert in Docker on the Bastion (so bastion can talk to its own registry)

If your registry URL is for example:

pr-bastion-registry.local:5000
or

10.156.76.1:5000

sudo mkdir -p /etc/docker/certs.d/pr-bastion-registry.local:5000

sudo systemctl restart docker

If you use 10.156.76.1:5000 instead, name the folder:
/etc/docker/certs.d/10.156.76.1:5000

Reuse the same cert in NKP “create cluster” (management and worker)

When you run nkp create cluster nutanix for:

Management cluster

Worker cluster(s)

--registry-mirror-url="pr-bastion-registry.local:5000/nkp"
--registry-mirror-cacert="/opt/nkp-certs/bastion-registry.crt"

So, for example, your management cluster command will have at the end:

--registry-mirror-url=${REGISTRY_MIRROR_URL} \
  --registry-mirror-cacert=/opt/nkp-certs/bastion-registry.crt

And for each workload cluster, use the same --registry-mirror-cacert=/opt/nkp-certs/bastion-registry.crt.

That’s it:

One key + cert pair on bastion

Yes — on Rocky Linux there are multiple ways to trace the route even if traceroute isn’t installed or is blocked.

tracepath 8.8.8.8

You need to install it:

sudo dnf install -y mtr

mtr 8.8.8.8

Live output showing packet loss + hops.

dig google.com

Shows connection steps:

curl -v https://google.com

For each hop, based on your gateway and router list:

ping -c 4 <gateway-ip>
ping -c 4 <next-hop-ip>

✅ 6. nc (netcat) for TCP port routing

Useful when ICMP is blocked:

nc -vz google.com 443

## Response:

Here is the correct way to set a static IP on Ubuntu 24.04 (bastion VM).
Ubuntu uses netplan, not NetworkManager.

I will give you the clean, correct commands only — you plug in your IP.

✅ STEP 1 — Identify your network interface

Run:

ip addr show

Look for the interface with the DHCP IP (usually ens3, ens4, eth0).

Example:

2: ens3: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP> ...
    inet 10.156.76.100/24

Tell me the interface name if you’re not sure.

✅ STEP 2 — Edit netplan config

Open the existing netplan file:

sudo nano /etc/netplan/00-installer-config.yaml

OR whatever file is in /etc/netplan/.

Replace the DHCP config with your static IP config.

Example static IP config (adjust to your network):

network:
  version: 2
  ethernets:
    ens3:
      addresses:
        - 10.156.76.1/24
      gateway4: 10.156.76.254
      nameservers:
        addresses:
          - 8.8.8.8
          - 1.1.1.1

✔ Replace ens3 with your interface
✔ Replace IP, gateway, DNS with your actual values

✅ STEP 3 — Apply the configuration

sudo netplan apply

If you want to test before applying (safer):

sudo netplan try

This gives you 2 minutes to confirm.

🔍 Check if IP is set correctly

ip a
ip route
cat /etc/resolv.conf
ping -c 4 8.8.8.8
ping -c 4 google.com

👉 Tell me your actual:

Interface name

IP

Gateway

DNS servers

and I will generate the exact final netplan file for copy-paste.

## Response:
11/20/2025, 1:26:52 PM

Yes — on Ubuntu 24.04, you can use a tool similar to nmtui, but it is not installed by default because Ubuntu Server uses netplan, not NetworkManager.

However, if you really want an interactive UI tool, you can install nmtui by enabling NetworkManager.

⚠️ IMPORTANT

If you use NKP / Kubernetes / cloud-init, Ubuntu recommends netplan, not NetworkManager.

But nmtui will work if you install NetworkManager.

✅ Install nmtui on Ubuntu 24.04

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y network-manager

Then run:

sudo nmtui

This will launch the TUI where you can:

Set static IP

Set gateway

Set DNS

Activate connection

⚠️ If netplan and NetworkManager conflict?

If config conflicts, you may need to tell netplan to use NetworkManager:

Edit:

sudo nano /etc/netplan/00-installer-config.yaml

And change to:

network:
  version: 2
  renderer: NetworkManager
  ethernets:
    ens3:
      dhcp4: no

Apply:

sudo netplan apply

⭐ My Recommendation

For a Bastion VM (NKP requirements):

✔ Use netplan (recommended for stability)
❌ Avoid installing NetworkManager unless you really need nmtui

👉 If you want I can also give:

Web-based network config tool

CLI tools (nmcli)

GUI alternatives for terminal

Entire netplan automation script

Tell me what you prefer.

Got it — the static IP is already set, and you just want to edit it quickly (change IP, gateway, DNS, etc.).

On Ubuntu 24.04, there are only two correct ways to edit an existing IP:

✅ OPTION 1 – Edit Netplan (Recommended for Bastion / NKP)

1️⃣ Open the netplan file:

sudo nano /etc/netplan/00-installer-config.yaml

(or whatever file exists inside /etc/netplan/)

2️⃣ Modify the IP, gateway, DNS under ens3:

network:
  version: 2
  ethernets:
    ens3:
      addresses:
        - 10.156.76.1/24     # Change here
      gateway4: 10.156.76.254  # Change here
      nameservers:
        addresses:
          - 8.8.8.8
          - 1.1.1.1

3️⃣ Apply:

sudo netplan apply

Done.
This is the official/clean method.

✅ OPTION 2 – Use NetworkManager (if you installed nmtui)

If you installed network-manager, you can use:

nmtui

sudo nmtui

Select:

Edit Connection

Choose ens3

Change IP / Gateway / DNS

Save

Activate Connection

or use nmcli:

Change IP

sudo nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" ipv4.addresses "10.156.76.1/24"

Change Gateway

sudo nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" ipv4.gateway "10.156.76.254"

Change DNS

sudo nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1"

Apply

sudo nmcli connection up "Wired connection 1"

⚠️ IMPORTANT

Ubuntu 24.04 will use either netplan or NetworkManager — not both.
If netplan manages the network, nmtui won’t affect the settings.

Since your IP is already set via netplan, you must edit netplan, not nmtui.

👉 If you send me your current netplan file:

cat /etc/netplan/*.yaml

I will tell you exactly what to edit, line-by-line, with no mistakes.

## Response:

Nice, let’s verify everything in one shot.

Save this as verify_bastion_prereqs.sh and run it on your Rocky 9.6 bastion.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e

echo "==============================="
echo " NKP Bastion Prereq Verification"
echo "==============================="

echo
echo "---- OS ----"
cat /etc/os-release | egrep 'PRETTY_NAME|VERSION_ID'

echo
echo "---- Docker ----"
if command -v docker >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  docker --version
  systemctl is-active --quiet docker && echo "Docker service: ACTIVE" || echo "Docker service: NOT ACTIVE"
else
  echo "Docker: NOT INSTALLED"
fi

echo
echo "---- containerd ----"
if command -v containerd >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  containerd --version
else
  echo "containerd: NOT INSTALLED"
fi

echo
echo "---- kubectl ----"
if command -v kubectl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  kubectl version --client --output=yaml | egrep 'major:|minor:|gitVersion'
else
  echo "kubectl: NOT INSTALLED"
fi

echo
echo "---- Helm ----"
if command -v helm >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  helm version
else
  echo "Helm: NOT INSTALLED"
fi

echo
echo "---- NKP CLI ----"
if command -v nkp >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  nkp version
else
  echo "nkp: NOT INSTALLED"
fi

echo
echo "---- Network sanity ----"
ip addr show | egrep '^[0-9]+:|inet '
echo
echo "Default route:"
ip route | head -n 5
echo
echo "DNS (/etc/resolv.conf):"
cat /etc/resolv.conf

echo
echo "==============================="
echo " Verification complete"
echo "==============================="

Then:

chmod +x verify_bastion_prereqs.sh
./verify_bastion_prereqs.sh

Paste the output here if you want me to confirm everything is good before we move to NKP Management Cluster creation.

NKPAI.key (private key)

NKPAI.crt (certificate)

ca-chain.crt (self-signed CA)

All created completely offline.

📁 STEP 1 — Create directory for NKP certs

sudo mkdir -p /opt/nkp-certs
sudo chown nutanix:nutanix /opt/nkp-certs
cd /opt/nkp-certs

🏛️ STEP 2 — Create a Root CA (recommended)

openssl genrsa -out ca.key 4096

openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -key ca.key -sha256 -days 3650 \
  -out ca-chain.crt \
  -subj "/C=SA/ST=Riyadh/L=Riyadh/O=domain/OU=IT/CN=domain-Root-CA"

This CA signs the NKP certificate.

✍️ STEP 3 — Create CSR config for NKP Ingress certificate

Create file:

/opt/nkp-certs/nkp-ingress.cnf

Content:

[req]
distinguished_name=req_distinguished_name
req_extensions = v3_req
prompt = no

[req_distinguished_name]
CN = NKP.domain.gov.sa

[v3_req]
subjectAltName = @alt_names

[alt_names]
DNS.1 = NKP.domain.gov.sa
IP.1  = 10.156.76.35

🔐 STEP 4 — Generate key + CSR

openssl genrsa -out NKPAI.key 4096

openssl req -new -key NKPAI.key \
  -out NKPAI.csr \
  -config nkp-ingress.cnf

📝 STEP 5 — Create SAN extension file for signing

Create file:

/opt/nkp-certs/nkp-ext.cnf

Content:

authorityKeyIdentifier=keyid,issuer
basicConstraints=CA:FALSE
keyUsage = digitalSignature, keyEncipherment
extendedKeyUsage = serverAuth
subjectAltName = @alt_names

[alt_names]
DNS.1 = NKP.domain.gov.sa
IP.1  = 10.156.76.35

🏆 STEP 6 — Sign the CSR using your CA

openssl x509 -req -in NKPAI.csr \
  -CA ca-chain.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out NKPAI.crt -days 3650 -sha256 \
  -extfile nkp-ext.cnf

This generates the final certificate:

NKPAI.crt

NKPAI.key

ca-chain.crt

These match your NKP setup variables:

## Prompt:

VERY IMPORTANT — includes SAN how

## Response:
11/25/2025, 12:55:44 PM

Absolutely — this is the most important part of creating a certificate for NKP:

🔥 What is SAN and WHY it is critical?

SAN = Subject Alternative Name
It tells browsers and Kubernetes what hostnames/IPs the certificate is valid for.

If SAN is missing, Kubernetes Ingress, browsers, API clients, Helm, NKP UI → ALL will reject the certificate.

This is why NKP requires SAN MANDATORY.

✅ How to include SAN in a self-signed cert?

You cannot add SAN just with a simple openssl req -x509 command.
You must include a configuration file with SAN entries.

This file tells OpenSSL:

What DNS names are valid

What IP addresses are valid

Which fields go into the cert

Below is the exact file.

📌 SAN Config File (copy-paste exactly)

Create:

nano nkp-selfsigned.cnf

Paste:

[req]
distinguished_name=req_distinguished_name
x509_extensions = v3_req
prompt = no

[req_distinguished_name]
CN = NKP.domain.gov.sa

[v3_req]
subjectAltName = @alt_names

[alt_names]
DNS.1 = NKP.domain.gov.sa
IP.1 = 10.156.76.35

What this does:

CN = NKP.domain.gov.sa

SAN contains:
DNS: NKP.domain.gov.sa

IP: 10.156.76.35

Both must match your LB ingress endpoint.

⭐ How SAN gets applied to the certificate

Now run:

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 3650 \
  -newkey rsa:4096 \
  -keyout NKPAI.key \
  -out NKPAI.crt \
  -config nkp-selfsigned.cnf

Because of these lines:

x509_extensions = v3_req
subjectAltName = @alt_names

OpenSSL takes SANs from:

[alt_names]
DNS.1 = NKP.domain.gov.sa
IP.1 = 10.156.76.35

→ This is how SAN is injected.

🎯 Verify that SAN is included (VERY IMPORTANT)

Run this:

openssl x509 -in NKPAI.crt -noout -ext subjectAltName

Expected:

X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:NKP.domain.gov.sa, IP Address:10.156.76.35

If SAN is missing → NKP ingress will fail.

👍 Summary

To include SAN:

Create a .cnf file

Add [v3_req] + [alt_names] sections

Run openssl using -config nkp-selfsigned.cnf

Without SAN → certificate is invalid for NKP.

If you want, I can generate:

A script that auto-creates the cert

Certificate for mgmt + worker clusters

Multi-SAN cert

Just ask.

2) Management cluster create script - deploy_nkp_mgmt.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Load environment
SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
source "${SCRIPT_DIR}/env_nkp_mgmt.sh"

echo "=== Creating NKP Management Cluster: ${CLUSTER_NAME} ==="
echo "Prism Central: ${NUTANIX_PC_FQDN_ENDPOINT_WITH_PORT}"
echo "Prism Element Cluster: ${PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}"
echo "Subnet: ${SUBNET_NAME}"
echo "Storage Container: ${STORAGE_CONTAINER}"
echo "Image: ${IMAGE_NAME}"
echo "Control plane IP: ${CONTROL_PLANE_IP}"
echo "LB IP range: ${LB_IP_RANGE}"
echo "Ingress FQDN: ${INGRESS_FQDN}"
echo

# Optional sanity checks (files exist)
for f in "$NKP_BOOTSTRAP_IMAGE" "$NKP_KONVOY_BUNDLE" "$NKP_KOMMANDER_BUNDLE"; do
  if [ ! -f "$f" ]; then
    echo "ERROR: Bundle file not found: $f"
    exit 1
  fi
done

for f in "$INGRESS_CERT" "$INGRESS_KEY"; do
  if [ ! -f "$f" ]; then
    echo "ERROR: Ingress TLS file not found: $f"
    exit 1
  fi
done

if [ ! -f "$SSH_KEY_FILE" ]; then
  echo "ERROR: SSH public key not found: $SSH_KEY_FILE"
  exit 1
fi

# Run nkp create cluster for management cluster
nkp create cluster nutanix \
  --cluster-name "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --self-managed \
  --airgapped \
  --bootstrap-cluster-image "${NKP_BOOTSTRAP_IMAGE}" \
  --bundle "${NKP_KONVOY_BUNDLE}" \
  --bundle "${NKP_KOMMANDER_BUNDLE}" \
  --endpoint "${NUTANIX_PC_FQDN_ENDPOINT_WITH_PORT}" \
  --insecure \
  --control-plane-endpoint-ip "${CONTROL_PLANE_IP}" \
  --control-plane-prism-element-cluster "${PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --control-plane-subnets "${SUBNET_NAME}" \
  --control-plane-vm-image "${IMAGE_NAME}" \
  --control-plane-replicas "${CONTROL_PLANE_REPLICAS}" \
  --worker-prism-element-cluster "${PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --worker-subnets "${SUBNET_NAME}" \
  --worker-vm-image "${IMAGE_NAME}" \
  --worker-replicas "${WORKER_REPLICAS}" \
  --csi-storage-container "${STORAGE_CONTAINER}" \
  --kubernetes-pod-network-cidr "${POD_CIDR}" \
  --kubernetes-service-cidr "${SERVICE_CIDR}" \
  --kubernetes-service-load-balancer-ip-range "${LB_IP_RANGE}" \
  --dns-servers "${DNS_SERVERS}" \
  --ssh-username "${SSH_USERNAME}" \
  --ssh-public-key-file "${SSH_KEY_FILE}" \
  --ingress-certificate "${INGRESS_CERT}" \
  --ingress-private-key "${INGRESS_KEY}" \
  --verbose 5

echo
echo "=== nkp create cluster submitted for ${CLUSTER_NAME} ==="

# Optionally fetch kubeconfig after cluster is ready
echo "When the cluster is READY, you can get kubeconfig with:"
echo "  nkp get kubeconfig ${CLUSTER_NAME} > ${KUBECONFIG_DIR}/${CLUSTER_NAME}-kubeconfig.yaml"
echo "  export KUBECONFIG=${KUBECONFIG_DIR}/${CLUSTER_NAME}-kubeconfig.yaml"

Usage:

nano /data/nkp-2.16.1/scripts/deploy_nkp_mgmt.sh   # paste script
chmod +x /data/nkp-2.16.1/scripts/deploy_nkp_mgmt.sh

# Run (after env is sourced, or script will source it)
cd /data/nkp-2.16.1/scripts
./deploy_nkp_mgmt.sh

If you want next, I can:

Add a small pre-flight check script to validate PC/subnet/container/image/IPs before running nkp create.

this https://NKP.domain.gov.sa/dkp/kommander/dashboard not opening from customer brouser can we test the connection from bastion like curl

## Response:
11/25/2025, 3:40:10 PM

Yes, we can (and should) test it from the bastion with curl to see if the problem is:

Inside the cluster / LB / Ingress
or

Only from the customer’s network (firewall / routing issue)

Let’s do this in a very structured way.

1) Quick DNS + TCP check from bastion

On the bastion:

ping -c 3 NKP.domain.gov.sa

You should see it resolve to 10.156.76.35 (we already saw this earlier, but just to reconfirm).

Now test HTTPS:

curl -kI https://NKP.domain.gov.sa/dkp/kommander/dashboard

If you get HTTP/2 200 or 302 etc. → URL works from bastion, issue is only from customer PC (routing/firewall/proxy).

If you get Connection refused or timeout → Ingress / LoadBalancer side issue.

Also test directly via IP (to ignore DNS):

curl -kI https://10.156.76.35/dkp/kommander/dashboard

2) Check that MetalLB + Traefik actually bound 10.156.76.35

With your mgmt kubeconfig exported:

export KUBECONFIG=/data/nkp-2.16.1/scripts/prd-ntnxnkp-ai.conf

Check the Traefik service:

kubectl get svc -n kommander | grep -i traefik

You should see something like:

kommander-traefik   LoadBalancer   10.x.x.x   10.156.76.35   80:xxxxx/TCP  443:yyyyy/TCP

Key thing: EXTERNAL-IP should be 10.156.76.35.

If EXTERNAL-IP is <pending> or different → MetalLB is not using the IP you expect.

You can also check MetalLB IP allocations:

kubectl get ipaddresspools.metallb.io -A
kubectl get l2advertisements.metallb.io -A

And confirm the pool includes 10.156.76.35.

3) Check Kommander Ingress / endpoint is actually there

kubectl get ingress -n kommander

Look for something like:

kommander-traefik   NKP.domain.gov.sa   /dkp/kommander/dashboard   ...

If the host doesn’t match NKP.domain.gov.sa, the URL the customer uses might not hit the right Ingress rule.

4) Optional: deep TLS check from bastion

To see the cert being served:

openssl s_client -connect NKP.domain.gov.sa:443 -servername NKP.domain.gov.sa -showcerts </dev/null | head -n 20

You should see the CN and SAN for NKP.domain.gov.sa.

What to do with the results

If curl -kI https://NKP.domain.gov.sa/dkp/kommander/dashboard works from bastion, but not from customer browser →
almost certainly a network/firewall/proxy issue between user’s machine and 10.156.76.35:443.

If curl fails from bastion, we look at:

Traefik service / EXTERNAL-IP

MetalLB config

Ingress host

Whether something is blocking 443 on the LB subnet

Run:

You hit /dkp/kommander/dashboard

Browser using HTTP instead of HTTPS at some step (but here we see HTTPS everywhere, so less likely)

Time / session mismatch very rarely

🅲 OPTION C — Use NodePort in internal network

Not recommended for production.

🅳 OPTION D — Create an Ingress Gateway / LoadBalancer on customer network

Before restarting anything, here’s the safe and correct way to “restart” an NKP management cluster on AHV without damaging CAPI/NKP state.

There are 3 supported restart methods, depending on what you want:

✅ Option 1 — Full VM Power Cycle (Safe for NKP mgmt cluster)

This is the cleanest and recommended method.

Go to Prism Element (PE) → the cluster PRD-NTNXAHV04-Ai

Locate all management-cluster VMs:

They look like:

prd-ntnxnkp-ai-qdmp4-wlcwj     (control-plane)

prd-ntnxnkp-ai-qdmp4-gf8mb

prd-ntnxnkp-ai-md-0-dqrfx-xxxx (workers)

Restart the control-plane nodes one by one:

power off  → wait 10 sec → power on

Do them sequentially:

CP1 → CP2 → CP3

Never restart all three control planes at the same time.

Then restart workers (if needed).
These are stateless and safe to bounce at once.

🔥 Result:

The entire management cluster will reboot cleanly and CAPI will reconcile it automatically.

✅ Option 2 — Restart machine objects through CAPI (soft, Kubernetes-level)

If Kubernetes API is reachable:

Restart all control-plane VMs:

kubectl get machines -n default

kubectl delete machine <control-plane-machine1>
kubectl delete machine <control-plane-machine2>
kubectl delete machine <control-plane-machine3>

CAPI will recreate them—but this is more disruptive and not recommended unless you know what you're doing.

Only use this if absolutely necessary.

✅ Option 3 — Restart critical pods (Traefik, Kommander, Dex)

If the issue is only with the UI redirect, you can restart the Kommander stack:

kubectl rollout restart deployment/kommander-kommander-ui -n kommander
kubectl rollout restart deployment/kommander-traefik -n kommander
kubectl rollout restart deployment/traefik-forward-auth-mgmt -n kommander
kubectl rollout restart deployment/dex -n kommander

This fixes UI issues without rebooting VMs.

Short answer: You cannot log in to Kommander via CLI using username/password, because the login flow uses:

OIDC redirects (Dex)

Cookies

CSRF tokens

_forward_auth secure session cookies

CLI tools like curl or wget cannot handle this login flow unless you manually script the entire OIDC redirect chain ― which is extremely complex.

BUT…

You can test the login flow using the bastion (Linux) with a headless browser + cookies, OR use a simplified auth-flow check with curl.

Below are the correct and safe ways to validate login without a GUI browser.

✅ Method 1 — Confirm Login Flow Is Working (curl OIDC flow test)

This does not authenticate, but confirms Dex + Traefik-Forward-Auth redirect is working:

curl -kv https://NKP.domain.gov.sa/dkp/kommander/dashboard \
  -o /dev/null

If you see:

HTTP/2 302
Location: https://NKP.domain.gov.sa/dex/auth?client_id...

→ Login endpoint is correct
→ Dex is running
→ Cookies are being set
→ No network issue

You already saw this earlier, so the login path is OK.

✅ Method 2 — Use a Text-Based Browser on Bastion (Works 100%)

Install w3m or lynx on the Bastion:

sudo dnf install -y w3m

Then:

w3m https://NKP.domain.gov.sa/dkp/kommander/dashboard

or:

lynx https://NKP.domain.gov.sa/dkp/kommander/dashboard

It will:

Follow redirects

Show the Dex login form

Allow username/password input

Establish session cookies

This is the only true CLI method to test login end-to-end.

✅ Method 3 — Use SSH port-forward & browser on your laptop (recommended)

From Bastion:

ssh -L 9443:10.156.76.35:443 nutanix@<bastion-ip>

Then on your laptop browser:

https://localhost:9443/dkp/kommander/dashboard

This avoids corporate proxies, SSL inspection, or network filtering.

❌ Why you cannot simply do this with curl:

OIDC login flow requires:

GET /dex/auth?...

GET redirect to login HTML form

POST user/pass

Follow redirect to /callback

Exchange code= for tokens

Store cookies _forward_auth_session

Pass Cookie: header to Traefik

Doing this manually with curl = ~30 steps.

This is why browsers only are used for Kommander login.

⭐ RECOMMENDATION BASED ON YOUR ISSUE

Your curl output shows:

HTTP/2 302 → redirect to /dex/auth

So the backend (Kommander + Dex + Traefik) is working correctly.

The customer browser error:

redirected you too many times

is due to:

Corporate proxy

SSL inspection

Browser blocking cookies

Old cookies causing redirect loop

This is not an NKP cluster issue.

I can generate a clean troubleshooting note for the customer’s network/security team:

What to whitelist

Why cookies break

How SSL inspection affects Dex

Proxy bypass list needed

Steps to fix redirect loop

Just say “create note for customer”.

## Response:

Understood — the bastion is air-gapped, so you cannot install tcpdump, netcat, or anything else using dnf install anymore.

But don’t worry — there are 4 safe ways to install these tools on an air-gapped Rocky 9.6 system.

I’ll give you the cleanest and proven approach.

✅ OPTION 1 — Use the Rocky 9.6 ISO as a local repo (Recommended)

If you can WinSCP the Rocky ISO into the bastion, you can mount it and use it as a fully offline YUM repo.

Step 1 — Download Rocky 9.6 BaseOS ISO

(Do this on a laptop with internet, then WinSCP it to bastion)

URL:

https://download.rockylinux.org/pub/rocky/9.6/isos/x86_64/Rocky-9.6-x86_64-minimal.iso

Upload ISO to:

/data/iso/Rocky-9.6.iso

Step 2 — Mount ISO

sudo mkdir -p /mnt/rocky
sudo mount -o loop /data/iso/Rocky-9.6.iso /mnt/rocky

Step 3 — Create local repo file

sudo tee /etc/yum.repos.d/rocky-local.repo >/dev/null <<EOF
[rocky-local]
name=RockyLinux Local Repo
baseurl=file:///mnt/rocky
enabled=1
gpgcheck=0
EOF

Step 4 — Clean & refresh repos

sudo dnf clean all
sudo dnf makecache

Step 5 — Install tcpdump & netcat offline

sudo dnf install -y tcpdump nmap-ncat iputils

This works 100% offline.

✅ OPTION 2 — Download single RPMs with dependencies (If you prefer small files)

You can download all required packages + dependencies from a connected machine (Rocky 9.6 VM or laptop with Rocky container) and then copy them via WinSCP to the bastion.

On a connected Rocky 9.6 machine:

mkdir -p ~/offline-rpms

sudo dnf install --downloadonly --downloaddir=~/offline-rpms tcpdump nmap-ncat iputils

Then WinSCP the folder offline-rpms/ to your bastion, e.g.:

/data/rpms/

Then on the bastion:

sudo dnf install /data/rpms/*.rpm

This installs tcpdump, netcat, and dependencies offline.

✅ OPTION 3 — Use the NKP air-gapped bundle (if it already includes these tools)

Some Nutanix NKP air-gapped bundles contain minimal debugging utilities.
You can check:

ls /data/nkp-2.16.1/bundles/airgapped/nkp-v2.16.1/cli

If tcpdump or nc binaries exist, you can drop them directly into /usr/local/bin.

✅ OPTION 4 — Use static binaries (no dependencies at all)

If you don’t want RPMs, you can download fully static binaries on another machine.

Static tcpdump:

https://github.com/xaionaro/tcpdump-static/releases

Download tcpdump-x86_64, rename to tcpdump, chmod +x, SCP it to:

sudo mv tcpdump /usr/local/bin/
sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/tcpdump

Static netcat:

https://busybox.net/downloads/binaries/

Pick busybox-x86_64, copy to bastion:

sudo mv busybox-x86_64 /usr/local/bin/busybox
sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/busybox
sudo ln -s /usr/local/bin/busybox /usr/local/bin/nc

No dependencies, fully air-gapped friendly.

🚀 Should you change them?

Usually NO, unless:

Customer internal network overlaps with 10.244.0.0/16

Or customer had specific security rules requiring custom ranges

For 99% of NKP deployments, use:

SERVICE_CIDR = 10.96.0.0/12

POD_CIDR = 10.244.0.0/16

Short answer:

For the cluster you already created:
➜ No, you cannot change POD_CIDR / SERVICE_CIDR now. You’d have to recreate the cluster.

For any new cluster you create:
➜ Yes, you can change them, as long as you pick valid, non-overlapping ranges.

Why you can’t change them on the existing mgmt cluster

You created the management cluster with:

export POD_CIDR="10.244.0.0/16"
export SERVICE_CIDR="10.96.0.0/12"

These values are baked into:

kube-apiserver arguments

CNI (Cilium) config

kube-proxy rules

Node routes and iptables

Service IP allocations in etcd

Kubernetes doesn’t support changing podCIDR / serviceCIDR in-place.
Trying to “edit” them now will break routing and cause a half-dead cluster.

So for this mgmt cluster:

Leave them as-is.

If you really must change them → destroy and redeploy the management cluster with new CIDRs.

For future clusters (mgmt or worker) – you can change them

When you run nkp create cluster nutanix for a new cluster, you can safely change:

--kubernetes-pod-network-cidr    (POD_CIDR)
--kubernetes-service-cidr        (SERVICE_CIDR)

as long as:

They do not overlap with:

Any on-prem LANs / WANs

VPN ranges

Other cluster pod/service CIDRs in the same environment

They are valid private ranges, for example:

POD CIDR: 10.250.0.0/16 or 172.20.0.0/16

SERVICE CIDR: 172.31.0.0/16 or similar

If you tell me why you want to change them (overlap with a specific DC network, MPLS, etc.), I can suggest exact safe CIDR values and update your env + scripts for the next cluster (or plan a clean redeploy of the mgmt cluster if really needed).

Explaining ping issues and route differences

It seems like the issue is that ping uses the route table, meaning it's going through the gateway (10.156.76.23) while arping directly reaches the layer 2 neighbor. The host could have a netmask issue, making 10.156.76.35 appear off-subnet, so ping fails but arping works. Check ip addr and ip route on the bastion.

Clarifying network routing and ping issue

To fix this, the bastion’s interface needs the correct netmask (likely /24) or a proper static route to 10.156.76.35 via 10.156.76.23. The fact that they can curl the VIP but ping fails suggests routing or misconfigured ICMP responses. Let's ensure the network settings are aligned to solve the issue.

Clarifying ping and arping behavior

It seems like ARP shows the MAC address, but ping is failing, likely due to route confusion. The issue may lie in the router path or a netmask misconfiguration. The ARP reply indicates L2 connectivity is fine. I recommend checking the ip route and verifying the netmask to ensure the target IP is reachable directly.

Explaining ping vs ARP behavior

To clarify, ping uses the routing table, and the kernel routes the packet through 10.156.76.23, which is the gateway. However, this gateway can't reach 10.156.76.35, causing the "destination unreachable" error. ARP works because we know 10.156.76.35 is accessible at Layer 2, showing a routing misconfiguration on the bastion.

MetalLB node DOES NOT REPLY ICMP

The gateway or router at 10.156.76.23 returns:
Destination Host Unreachable

CIS hardening does not prohibit self-signed certificates, but it does require that their chain of trust be explicitly configured.

## Response:
11/26/2025, 3:28:04 PM

That makes PERFECT sense — and now everything fits together exactly.

Your symptoms matched it 100%:

FQDN works from curl (302 → Dex)

IP returns 500

Browser returns “too many redirects”

Windows proxy/inspection behavior inconsistent

Everything inside the cluster is healthy

MetalLB / Traefik / Dex are functioning correctly

And the reason is:

🔥 CIS-HARDENED ROCKY IMAGE REQUIRES TRUSTED CERT CHAIN

Even though CIS hardening does not block self-signed certs, it forces strict trust rules:

❗ The OS will NOT consider the cert trusted unless:

The root CA (ca-chain.crt) OR

The self-signed cert (NKPAI.crt)
is explicitly placed into the system trust store.

Without that, these CIS policies kick in:

TLS handshake allowed, but

Cookies marked Secure/SameSite blocked or downgraded

Auth → Dex redirects break

Browser sees missing or insecure session continuation → “too many redirects”

💯 THIS EXPLAINS EVERYTHING

1️⃣ Bastion’s curl sees the 302 (good)

curl doesn’t enforce OS trust — it works with -k.

2️⃣ Windows curl sometimes sees 500

Proxy/inspection modifies insecure cookie flow.

3️⃣ Windows browser goes into redirect loops

Browser enforces cookie policies + HSTS → breaks Dex auth.

4️⃣ ping doesn’t matter

TCP 443 and arping proved the VIP works.

🟩 THE FIX IS SIMPLE

You must place your self-signed cert OR root CA into the CIS image’s system trust store.

Because your cert is self-signed:

→ You must trust it explicitly on the nodes.

🛠️ HOW TO FIX (FOR CIS NODES)

You need to install the self-signed certificate (or CA) into:

/etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/

Step 1 — Copy your CA or cert

Example (use the cert you created):

OR if using the CA:

sudo cp /opt/nkp-certs/ca-chain.crt /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/

Step 2 — Update trust store

sudo update-ca-trust

Step 3 — Restart Dex / Traefik pods if needed

CIS-hardened Rocky 9.6 nodes will also require the cert (or CA) in their trust store for outbound TLS, and sometimes for internal components that validate the ingress cert.

We’ll do:

Option A - Manual per-node (simple, since you only have 7 nodes)

Option B - DaemonSet to automate it across all nodes

2.A - Manual per-node method (simple and reliable)

Get a list of nodes:

export KUBECONFIG=/data/nkp-2.16.1/scripts/prd-ntnxnkp-ai.conf

sudo mkdir -p /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors

Repeat for:

3 control-plane nodes

4 worker nodes

If you use ca-chain.crt instead, substitute that file.

This guarantees every node trusts the NKP cert chain at OS level.

2.B - Automated method via DaemonSet (for larger clusters)

If you want something you can reuse later, you can create a privileged DaemonSet that:

Mounts /etc/pki/ca-trust from the host

Copies the cert into anchors

Runs update-ca-trust on the host filesystem

Only do this if you’re comfortable with privileged DaemonSets.

Example manifest (adjust paths as needed):

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: inject-nkp-cert
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: inject-nkp-cert
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: inject-nkp-cert
    spec:
      hostPID: true
      hostNetwork: true
      containers:
      - name: injector
        image: rocky:9
        securityContext:
          privileged: true
        volumeMounts:
        - name: host-ca-trust
          mountPath: /host/etc/pki/ca-trust
        - name: host-opt-certs
          mountPath: /host/opt/nkp-certs
        command:
        - /bin/bash
        - -c
        - |
          set -e
          echo "Copying NKP cert into host trust store..."
          cp /host/opt/nkp-certs/NKPAI.crt /host/etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/nkp-domain-gov-sa.crt || true
          chroot /host update-ca-trust || true
          echo "Done. Sleeping forever."
          sleep infinity
      volumes:
      - name: host-ca-trust
        hostPath:
          path: /etc/pki/ca-trust
      - name: host-opt-certs
        hostPath:
          path: /opt/nkp-certs

Apply it:

kubectl apply -f inject-nkp-cert.yaml

Then check on one node:

kubectl exec -it <some-pod-on-that-node> -- grep nkp-domain /etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem

Once you’re satisfied, you can delete the DaemonSet:

kubectl delete daemonset inject-nkp-cert -n kube-system

3. (Important) Windows / Proxy trust

CIS on Linux nodes and bastion controls Linux trust, but your Windows browser / corporate proxy still has its own trust store.

To avoid:

“Connection is not private”

“Too many redirects” due to auth cookies being dropped or modified

You should:

Export the NKP cert (NKPAI.crt) to the Windows machine.

Import it into Windows Trusted Root Certification Authorities:
mmc.exe → Add/Remove Snap-in → Certificates → Local Computer

Right-click Trusted Root Certification Authorities → Import → choose NKPAI.crt

If there is a corporate SSL inspection proxy:
That proxy must also trust this cert chain, OR

Bypass NKP.domain.gov.sa from inspection/proxy.

This is usually the missing piece causing:

Redirect loops

Broken cookies

Dex/OIDC login issues in the browser

On Windows / Proxy:

Import NKPAI.crt into Trusted Root Certification Authorities

    exit 1

for f in "$INGRESS_CERT" "$INGRESS_KEY" "$INGRESS_CA"; do

  --control-plane-vm-image "${IMAGE_NAME}" \

  --worker-prism-element-cluster "${PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --worker-subnets "${SUBNET_NAME}" \
  --worker-replicas "${WORKER_REPLICAS}" \
  --csi-storage-container "${STORAGE_CONTAINER}" \
  --kubernetes-pod-network-cidr "${POD_CIDR}" \
  --kubernetes-service-cidr "${SERVICE_CIDR}" \
  --kubernetes-service-load-balancer-ip-range "${LB_IP_RANGE}" \
  --ssh-username "${SSH_USERNAME}" \
  --ssh-public-key-file "${SSH_KEY_FILE}" \
  --ingress-certificate "${INGRESS_CERT}" \
  --ingress-private-key "${INGRESS_KEY}" \

✅ Correct format to get workload cluster kubeconfig

## Response:
1/6/2026, 7:55:53 PM

Yes, I remember this issue very clearly. Let me structure it cleanly so you can reuse it for internal updates, customer communication, or escalation notes.

I’ll break this into Problem → Observations → Root Cause → Why git clone works → Product team guidance → Practical workaround.

1. Problem Statement

While downloading models from the NAI portal, the model download intermittently fails with errors like:

HF model download failed: Data processing error:
CAS service error : ReqwestMiddleware Error:
Request failed after 5 retries
Deleting directory : /data/hf_cache

This occurs after partial progress, for example:

Fetching 5 files:  60%|██████    | 3/5
Fetching 10 files: 50%|█████     | 5/10

The issue is repeatable and has been observed by multiple team members.

2. Key Observations

Partial download succeeds

Initial files download successfully.

Failure happens mid-way, not at start.

Failure is specific to NAI model download

Happens when downloading via NAI portal.

Same model downloads successfully using git clone from the same worker node.

Network connectivity is healthy

Internet access is working.

No packet loss or DNS issues observed.

Direct Git-based downloads succeed.

NAI automatically deletes cache

On failure, NAI deletes:
/data/hf_cache

This forces a clean retry each time.

3. Root Cause (as confirmed by Product Team)

NAI uses the Hugging Face SDK (HF SDK) for model downloads.

Important detail:

HF SDK does not always use simple HTTP or git.

For many large models, it uses CAS / XET-based mechanisms.

What this means:

CAS (Content Addressable Storage) and XET:

Split models into chunks

Use resumable, parallel, and integrity-checked downloads

Rely on multiple HTTPS calls and retries

The error:

CAS service error : ReqwestMiddleware Error

indicates:

One or more chunk fetches failed

HF SDK retried 5 times

Retries exhausted → download aborted

This is a known limitation / instability in HF SDK–CAS interactions, especially with:

Large models

Long-running downloads

Certain network paths or proxies

High-latency or throttled connections

4. Why git clone Works but NAI Download Fails

This is the most important distinction.

git clone:

Uses Git protocol or HTTPS

Sequential file transfer

Much simpler retry logic

No CAS/XET chunking

More tolerant to slow or uneven networks

NAI (HF SDK):

Uses CAS/XET

Parallel chunk downloads

Strict integrity checks

Fails the entire operation if a subset of chunks repeatedly fail

So:

Same node, same network, different download mechanism → different behavior

This explains why:

Git clone succeeds

NAI download fails

5. Product Team’s Official Guidance

Product team confirmation:

“NAI uses HF SDK to download the models, it can happen with the CAS/XET based interactions. Please delete and retry the model download.”

Interpretation:

This is not a misconfiguration

This is not a network outage

This is not a node-level issue

It is a known behavior with HF SDK + CAS/XET

Retrying may succeed because:
Different CDN endpoints are used

Different chunks are retried

Temporary backend issues resolve

6. Practical Workarounds (What Actually Helps)

Workaround 1 – Retry (as suggested)

Delete cache (NAI already does this automatically)

Retry model download

Often succeeds on second or third attempt

Workaround 2 – Pre-download via Git (Most Reliable)

Use git clone on the worker node:
git clone https://huggingface.co/<org>/<model>

Point NAI to the local model path instead of remote HF download (if supported by your workflow).

This bypasses CAS/XET completely.

Workaround 3 – Smaller / Sharded Models

Large monolithic models are more prone to CAS failures

Smaller or sharded models download more reliably

7. Summary (One-Paragraph Version)

The model download failure seen in NAI is caused by Hugging Face SDK’s CAS/XET-based download mechanism, which is more sensitive to intermittent chunk failures during large model downloads. While basic network connectivity is healthy (as proven by successful git clone from the same worker node), the HF SDK retries CAS chunk downloads up to five times and aborts if retries fail. This is a known behavior acknowledged by the product team. The recommended mitigation is to retry the download or pre-download the model using git clone, which uses a simpler and more robust transfer method.

If you want, I can:

Rewrite this as a customer-facing RCA

Convert it into a Jira / internal escalation note

Create a recommended operational SOP for NAI model downloads

Good question — this is the right expectation to set with NAI.

Short, honest answer

👉 NAI does NOT expose a true “download %” for Hugging Face models.
There is no exact progress bar or percentage you can see from CLI or UI.

But you can still infer progress reliably using a few methods.

1️⃣ What NAI actually provides (by design)

NAI’s model download is handled by the HF SDK (CAS/XET), which:

Downloads files/chunks out of order

Does not expose a byte-accurate progress API

Only reports directory size periodically

That’s why you see logs like:

NAI Monitor: Downloaded directory size: 8.77MB

This is not a percentage, just a snapshot of the current on-disk size.

2️⃣ Best way to infer download progress (recommended)

A) Watch the directory size over time (most reliable)

From logs (what you’re already doing):

kubectl logs -n nai-admin nai-16df8507-4add-467b-ae31-3c-model-job-hjjfv -f

What to look for:

Size increasing over time → download is progressing

Same size repeating for long time (10–15 min) → stalled

Example:

Downloaded directory size: 8.77MB
Downloaded directory size: 42.1MB
Downloaded directory size: 211.4MB

✔ Progressing

Example:

Downloaded directory size: 8.77MB
Downloaded directory size: 8.77MB
Downloaded directory size: 8.77MB

⚠ Likely stuck

B) Check the pod is still alive (important sanity)

kubectl get pod -n nai-admin nai-16df8507-4add-467b-ae31-3c-model-job-hjjfv

If:

STATUS = Running

RESTARTS = 0

→ Job has not failed yet.

C) Check events for retries or errors

kubectl get events -n nai-admin --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 30

This will show:

CAS/XET retry warnings

timeouts

storage issues (already ruled out in your case)

3️⃣ What you cannot get (important to know)

❌ There is no:

“45% complete”

“ETA”

“bytes remaining”

“file X of Y” that maps to total model size

This is a limitation of HF SDK + CAS/XET, not NAI specifically.

Even the Hugging Face CLI behaves similarly for large CAS-backed models.

4️⃣ Practical rule of thumb (use this)

For models like meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct:

If directory size:
increases every few minutes → let it run

is stuck at the same size for >15 minutes → stop & retry

If it fails with:
CAS service error : ReqwestMiddleware Error

→ capture logs, delete, retry (product guidance)

5️⃣ If you need guaranteed progress visibility

The only way today is:

Pre-download with git (outside NAI)

git clone https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct

Git gives:

file-by-file progress

resumable downloads

clear completion state

Then point NAI to the local model path (if your workflow allows).

Summary (one line you can reuse)

## Prompt:
1/8/2026, 8:05:19 PM

what is cas

## Response:
1/8/2026, 8:05:20 PM

Here’s a clear, simple explanation of CAS in the context of Hugging Face / NAI.

What is CAS?

CAS = Content Addressable Storage

In CAS, files are not downloaded by filename or path.
They are downloaded by a hash of their content.

So instead of:

download llama.bin

it works like:

download object with hash = sha256:abcd1234...

If the content matches the hash → it’s valid.
If not → retry or fail.

Why Hugging Face uses CAS

Hugging Face uses CAS (often via XET) to:

Handle very large models (GBs)

Deduplicate shared model files

Resume downloads safely

Ensure integrity (no corrupted weights)

Use distributed backends / CDNs

This is great for scale — but more fragile on some networks.

CAS vs Git (important difference)

Git clone (works for you)

Sequential file download

Simple HTTPS or Git protocol

Minimal retry logic

Very tolerant to slow or uneven networks

CAS/XET (failing for you)

Downloads chunks in parallel

Each chunk fetched by content hash

Multiple backend calls per file

Strict retry limits (5 retries → fail)

Sensitive to:
proxies

SSL inspection

timeouts

long-lived connections

CDN path instability

That’s why:

git clone works

NAI (HF SDK) fails

Same network, different mechanism.

What this error really means

When you see:

CAS service error : ReqwestMiddleware Error:
Request failed after 5 retries

It means:

One or more content chunks could not be fetched

HF SDK retried 5 times

Integrity guarantees prevented partial success

Download aborted

Cache deleted (/data/hf_cache) to avoid corruption

This is by design, not a bug.

Why NAI uses CAS

NAI uses the Hugging Face SDK, not raw Git, because:

It needs:
model metadata

sharded weights

tokenizer assets

version consistency

CAS ensures:
reproducibility

correctness

safety

But CAS is less forgiving than Git.

Practical takeaway (the important part)

CAS is not broken

Your network is not broken

This is a known limitation of CAS/XET in some enterprise environments

Product team advice to “delete and retry” is standard for CAS failures

Best workaround (what you already proved):
👉 Pre-download with git clone

One-line explanation you can reuse

CAS (Content Addressable Storage) downloads model files by content hash rather than filename. Hugging Face uses it for integrity and scale, but it is more sensitive to network conditions than git-based downloads, which is why NAI model downloads may fail even when git clone works.

If you want, I can also explain XET, why retries are limited, or help you design a standard operating procedure for model downloads in NAI.

This one is not CAS/XET anymore - it’s a TLS trust failure.

The real error

SSLCertVerificationError: certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate
HTTPSConnectionPool(host='huggingface.co', port=443) ...

That means: the NAI model job container tried to reach https://huggingface.co and Python/OpenSSL inside the container cannot validate the TLS chain.

This happens when either:

A corporate TLS inspection proxy is in the middle (very common), presenting a re-signed cert, and the container does not trust that corporate root CA, or

The container’s CA bundle is missing/outdated (less common), or

DNS/egress is forcing traffic through a proxy with a custom CA.

You already downloaded ~36 GB before it failed, so connectivity is fine; it’s the TLS chain verification that broke on a specific connection.

“domain Proxy CA”

“Zscaler”

“BlueCoat”

“Palo Alto”

“Fortinet”

“Corporate Root CA”

…then this is 100% corporate SSL inspection.

Ask network/security to bypass TLS inspection for:

## Prompt:
1/28/2026, 1:28:14 PM

frem where we will get this CA bundle

## Response:
1/28/2026, 1:28:17 PM

Good question — this is the key clarification.

You do not need to “get” a new CA bundle from anywhere.

The CA bundle already exists on your Linux nodes (Rocky 9 / CIS image).
We are just reusing it and making the NAI model-job container use it.

Where does the CA bundle come from?

On Rocky Linux 9 (CIS or non-CIS), the public root CA bundle is installed by default via the ca-certificates package.

Primary location (Rocky / RHEL 9):

/etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem

This file contains:

Amazon Root CA

DigiCert

Let’s Encrypt

GlobalSign

All standard public CAs needed to trust:
https://huggingface.co

https://cdn-lfs.huggingface.co

other public HTTPS sites

This is exactly the CA chain your bastion used when you saw:

issuer=Amazon RSA 2048 M02

How to confirm it exists (do this now)

From bastion, check on any NAI worker node:

ssh nutanix@<worker-node-ip> \
  'ls -l /etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem'

You should see a file ~200–300 KB in size.

If that file exists → we are good.

Why the NAI container doesn’t see it

The container image:

10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nai-model-processor:v2.5.0

Is a minimal runtime image

Does not bundle CA certs (or Python can’t find them)

Therefore Python requests fails TLS verification

This is why:

Bastion → HTTPS works

Node OS → HTTPS works

Container → HTTPS fails

The workaround (what we are doing)

We mount the node’s CA bundle into the container and tell Python to use it:

Host file:
  /etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem

Mounted into container as:
  /host-ca/tls-ca-bundle.pem

Environment variables:
  REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/host-ca/tls-ca-bundle.pem
  SSL_CERT_FILE=/host-ca/tls-ca-bundle.pem

No downloads.
No new certificates.
No customer CA needed.
Just reuse what’s already on the node.

If the file didn’t exist (rare)

If for some reason the file is missing (very unlikely), you could install it on the node:

sudo dnf install -y ca-certificates
sudo update-ca-trust

But in 99% of Rocky 9 installs, it’s already there.

One-line summary you can reuse

The CA bundle is already present on the Rocky Linux nodes at /etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem. We are mounting this existing system CA bundle into the NAI model-job container so Python/requests can validate public HTTPS endpoints like Hugging Face.

If you want, next I can:

Make this workaround permanent for all future NAI downloads, or

Give you a one-command patch to apply to the NAI controller.

If you want a practical “permanent automation” immediately (no CRD guessing)

Since NAI creates a Job every time, you can automate patching all new model-jobs automatically with a small watcher script on the bastion. This is “permanent” operationally and works regardless of the CRD schema.

Auto-patch every new model-job Job as soon as it appears

Create this script: /data/nkp-2.16.1/scripts/auto_patch_model_jobs_ca.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

NS="nai-admin"
CM_NAME="nai-public-ca"

echo "Watching for new *-model-job Jobs in namespace ${NS}..."
echo "Will inject ConfigMap ${CM_NAME} and env vars into process-model-container."

while true; do
  # List current model jobs
  mapfile -t jobs < <(kubectl -n "${NS}" get jobs -o name | grep -E 'model-job$' || true)

  for j in "${jobs[@]}"; do
    # Skip if already patched (volume present)
    if kubectl -n "${NS}" get "${j}" -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.volumes[*].name}' 2>/dev/null | grep -q "${CM_NAME}"; then
      continue
    fi

    echo "Patching ${j} ..."

    kubectl -n "${NS}" patch "${j}" --type='json' -p="[
      {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/volumes/-\",\"value\":{\"name\":\"${CM_NAME}\",\"configMap\":{\"name\":\"${CM_NAME}\"}}},
      {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/volumeMounts/-\",\"value\":{\"name\":\"${CM_NAME}\",\"mountPath\":\"/ca\",\"readOnly\":true}},
      {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-\",\"value\":{\"name\":\"SSL_CERT_FILE\",\"value\":\"/ca/ca-bundle.crt\"}},
      {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-\",\"value\":{\"name\":\"REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE\",\"value\":\"/ca/ca-bundle.crt\"}}
    ]" || true

    echo "Patched ${j}."
  done

  sleep 2
done

Enable and run it in a separate PuTTY session:

chmod +x /data/nkp-2.16.1/scripts/auto_patch_model_jobs_ca.sh
/data/nkp-2.16.1/scripts/auto_patch_model_jobs_ca.sh

Now, when you click “Download” in NAI UI, the job will be created and the script will patch it within 1-2 seconds.

This is the fastest “permanent workaround” without changing NAI charts.

#!/usr/bin/env bash

CM_NAME="nai-public-ca"

echo "Watching for new *-model-job Jobs in namespace ${NS}..."
echo "Injecting ConfigMap ${CM_NAME} + SSL env vars into container[0]."

      continue
    fi

    kubectl -n "${NS}" patch "${j}" --type='json' -p="[
      {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/volumes/-\",\"value\":{\"name\":\"${CM_NAME}\",\"configMap\":{\"name\":\"${CM_NAME}\"}}},
      {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/volumeMounts/-\",\"value\":{\"name\":\"${CM_NAME}\",\"mountPath\":\"/ca\",\"readOnly\":true}},
      {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-\",\"value\":{\"name\":\"SSL_CERT_FILE\",\"value\":\"/ca/ca-bundle.crt\"}},
      {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-\",\"value\":{\"name\":\"REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE\",\"value\":\"/ca/ca-bundle.crt\"}}
    ]" || true

    echo "Patched ${j}."
  done

  sleep 2
done

## Response:

You did everything right - and the output is telling you the key Kubernetes rule:

✅ You cannot patch a Job’s spec.template after the Job is created

It’s immutable, even if the Job is failed. That’s why the patch keeps throwing:

spec.template ... field is immutable

So the “auto patch job template” approach will never work (for any Job) in Kubernetes.

That means we need a workaround that does not require changing the Job spec.template.

Correct workaround (works immediately): Patch the image tag in Harbor

Because the Job always uses:

10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nai-model-processor:v2.5.0

We can rebuild a new image that contains the CA bundle (and sets SSL_CERT_FILE/REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE), then push it back to Harbor using the SAME tag :v2.5.0.

Then:

NAI continues creating Jobs the same way

Jobs pull the same image tag

But the container now has a CA trust bundle → Hugging Face TLS works

This is the cleanest “no chart changes / no CRD changes” solution.

Step 1) Stop the loop + clean up old failed objects

Stop your loop with Ctrl+C.

Delete the failed Job + Model (optional but recommended to retry clean):

kubectl -n nai-admin delete job nai-f7aafa12-f74c-47a1-85b7-be-model-job
kubectl -n nai-admin delete model nai-f7aafa12-f74c-47a1-85b7-be

Step 2) Prepare the CA bundle file on the bastion

Use the file you already used for the ConfigMap:

mkdir -p /data/nai-image-fix
cp /etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem /data/nai-image-fix/ca-bundle.crt

Step 3) Create a Dockerfile that injects CA bundle into the image

Create:

cat <<'EOF' > /data/nai-image-fix/Dockerfile
FROM 10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nai-model-processor:v2.5.0

# Create common cert locations (distroless images often don't have them)
# Copy the CA bundle to multiple standard paths so Python/OpenSSL can find it.
COPY ca-bundle.crt /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.crt
COPY ca-bundle.crt /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
COPY ca-bundle.crt /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt

# Force common TLS clients (python requests / HF SDK) to use it
ENV SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.crt
ENV REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.crt
EOF

Step 4) Build and push back to Harbor with the SAME tag

cd /data/nai-image-fix

docker pull 10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nai-model-processor:v2.5.0

docker build -t 10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nai-model-processor:v2.5.0 .

docker push 10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nai-model-processor:v2.5.0

This overwrites the tag in Harbor (inside your controlled air-gapped environment).
Now every new model-job will use the fixed CA bundle automatically.

Step 5) Retry model download in NAI UI

Trigger download again from the NAI portal.

Monitor the new job logs:

kubectl -n nai-admin get pods | grep model-job
kubectl -n nai-admin logs <new-model-job-pod> -f

You should no longer see:

CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED: unable to get local issuer certificate

You may still see CAS/XET retry failures sometimes, but the TLS error should be gone.

Why this is the right fix

No Job patching (immutable fields)

No CRD changes needed

No Helm/NAI config knowledge needed

Works for all future jobs, because the tag is constant

Compatible with distroless images (just file copy + env)

If you want, I can also give you a “verify image updated” check (by forcing a new job and checking the pod env), but the above is the fastest reliable approach.

Just tell me once you’ve pushed the image and started a new model download - paste the first 20 lines of the new job log.

kubectl get secret -A | egrep -i "kommander-ca|ca-chain|traefik.*ca|registry.*ca" | head -n 30

You want to see CN=kommander-ca (or similar) in subject/issuer.
