Thought for 42s

Got it - since Docker still won’t trust the registry for the token endpoint even after adding both CAs, the fastest way forward is to bypass Docker’s TLS verification entirely for pull/push by using skopeo (it supports --tls-verify=false cleanly).

This is also the exact workaround you’ve used before in air-gapped / internal-CA registries.

Why this works

docker pull/push is failing at /service/token TLS verification.

skopeo copy --src-tls-verify=false / --dest-tls-verify=false ignores that and will still authenticate with credentials.

Step 1) Install skopeo on bastion (since you have internet now)

sudo dnf install -y skopeo

Verify:

skopeo --version

Step 2) Pull the base image into the local Docker daemon (TLS verify disabled)

skopeo copy \
  --src-creds nutanix:'Nutanix/4u' \
  --src-tls-verify=false \
  docker://10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nai-model-processor:v2.5.0 \
  docker-daemon:nai-model-processor:v2.5.0

Confirm it exists locally:

docker images | grep nai-model-processor

Step 3) Update Dockerfile to use the local base image (not the registry URL)

Edit ~/nai-image-fix/Dockerfile and change line 1 to:

FROM nai-model-processor:v2.5.0

(keep the COPY + ENV lines the same)

Step 4) Build the patched image locally

cd ~/nai-image-fix
docker build -t nai-model-processor:v2.5.0-ca .

Step 5) Push the patched image back to registry using skopeo (TLS verify disabled)

First tag it in docker:

docker tag nai-model-processor:v2.5.0-ca 10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nai-model-processor:v2.5.0

Now push with skopeo:

skopeo copy \
  --dest-creds nutanix:'Nutanix/4u' \
  --dest-tls-verify=false \
  docker-daemon:10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nai-model-processor:v2.5.0 \
  docker://10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nai-model-processor:v2.5.0

This overwrites the tag in Harbor/registry.

Step 6) Retry model download in NAI UI

Now new model-jobs will use the same tag v2.5.0, but with CA bundle injected.

Monitor the new model-job logs; the goal is that this disappears:

CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED: unable to get local issuer certificate

Quick safety note

This skopeo method changes nothing in NKP/NAI configs; it only updates the image contents behind the same tag. That’s why it’s the most pragmatic workaround in your environment.

If you run Step 2 and it succeeds, paste the last 5 lines of output and we’ll proceed immediately to Step 3-5.

The CA cert in harbor-registry-ca is not actually the CA (it might be the wrong cert, or missing proper CA extensions), or

The registry is serving a cert chain that requires a different CA than we think, or

The CA bundle format/key is wrong for Flux (ca.crt must contain a PEM CA cert), or

## Response:
1/31/2026, 3:33:59 PM

Yes - in a proper air-gapped build, this driver image should come from an offline bundle, but it is usually NOT inside the NAI application bundle.

Why

The NAI bundle mainly carries NAI platform images and some common dependencies.

The GPU driver container (nvcr.io/nvidia/driver:580.82.07-ubuntu22.04) is part of NVIDIA GPU Operator / NGC, and is often handled separately (either by:
a GPU-operator offline bundle, or

a pre-mirrored driver container set,

or Nutanix LCM NVIDIA pack if you’re using that method).

Your timeouts to layers.nvcr.io are exactly what happens when you try to mirror the driver container live over a flaky path.

So the right move is:

First check whether the driver image already exists in any offline tar you have (NKP/NAI/GPU-operator bundle),

If yes → push from tar to Harbor (no internet involved),

If no → use another driver tag already in Harbor OR get the correct offline GPU operator/driver bundle.

Step A - Check if the driver image exists in any tar you already have

On bastion, search tars under your bundle directories:

# search in common locations (adjust if your bundle dir differs)

If you have a tar that likely contains NVIDIA images, we can list its contents.

Examples:

If it’s a “docker save” tar (single tar with manifest.json)

tar -tf <file>.tar | head
tar -xf <file>.tar manifest.json -O | head

If it’s an “OCI-archive” tar

tar -tf <file>.tar | head -n 50

You did the patch correctly, but the value keeps snapping back to just:

driver:
  enabled: true

That means this ConfigMap is being reconciled/overwritten by Flux/Kommander (it’s managed content). So any direct patch gets reverted almost immediately.

So we must update it at the reconciliation source - the Git/Flux kustomization that creates this ConfigMap, just like we did earlier for the OCIRepository.

Good news: we already know who owns it

The ConfigMap has labels pointing to the apps kustomization:

kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/name: apps-prd-ntnxnai-ai-wsvxj-cnqqg

So the fix is: patch the Kustomization that applies the overrides ConfigMap to include your repository + version.

✅ Step 1) Patch the Kustomization that manages the app overrides ConfigMap

First, show the kustomization YAML so we patch the right place:

kubectl -n prd-ntnxnai-ai-wsvxj-cnqqg get kustomization apps-prd-ntnxnai-ai-wsvxj-cnqqg -o yaml | sed -n '1,260p'

In that output, we’re looking for a section that references:

nvidia-gpu-operator-config-overrides

or a patch block for that ConfigMap

✅ Step 2) Quick workaround (if you want immediate effect)

Instead of fighting the ConfigMap, we can patch the HelmRelease values directly (also reconciled, but easier to patch with a postBuild patch).

Your kustomization nvidia-gpu-operator-helmrelease already has a patch that adds:

valuesFrom:
- kind: ConfigMap
  name: nvidia-gpu-operator-config-overrides

So if we can’t modify the ConfigMap, we can add an additional values block into the HelmRelease using the same kustomization patches.

That’s the most direct and durable fix.

Durable fix: Patch HelmRelease values in the same kustomization

We’ll add a second patch in nvidia-gpu-operator-helmrelease that injects the driver repo+version into the HelmRelease values.

Run:

kubectl -n prd-ntnxnai-ai-wsvxj-cnqqg patch kustomization nvidia-gpu-operator-helmrelease --type='json' -p='[
  {
    "op":"add",
    "path":"/spec/patches/-",
    "value":{
      "patch":"- op: add\n  path: /spec/values\n  value:\n    driver:\n      enabled: true\n      repository: 10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nvidia/driver\n      version: \"535-5.15.0-139-generic-ubuntu22.04\"\n",
      "target":{"kind":"HelmRelease","name":"nvidia-gpu-operator"}
    }
  }
]'

Then force reconcile:

kubectl -n prd-ntnxnai-ai-wsvxj-cnqqg annotate kustomization nvidia-gpu-operator-helmrelease \
  reconcile.fluxcd.io/requestedAt="$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" --overwrite

Now verify the HelmRelease values include your driver settings:

Most common causes in NKP/NAI environments:

That node is reaching a different Harbor VIP/ingress routing path that doesn’t have the new repo cached yet (rare).

That “Unavailable” entry is almost always a stale/failed Hugging Face import record — the download/verification job failed at some point, and the UI keeps the instance row even though the model object/pvc may be gone or partial.

In your case, it matches exactly what we saw earlier with Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct HF downloads failing (CAS/XET retries, and later TLS/CA issues). So the UI is showing:

Model Instance exists in NAI catalog state

Backend import status is failed → Unavailable

While other models are fine → Ready

Typical causes for “Unavailable” (most likely → least)

HF import job failed (CAS/XET timeout/retry exhausted, or TLS verify failure)

Partial download cleaned up (Deleting directory: /data/hf_cache) leaving no usable artifact

PVC/model files missing (PVC deleted, NFS hiccup, or cleanup happened)

Auth token issue (HF token expired/permission)

Network egress intermittency (less likely now that GPU + cluster is stable, but HF is still sensitive)

What to do now (fast + safe)

We should identify the actual Kubernetes Model object (if it exists) and its last failure reason, then delete/retry clean.

1) Find which Model CR corresponds to that Unavailable instance

Run:

export KUBECONFIG=/data/nkp-2.16.1/kubeconfigs/prd-ntnxnai-ai-kubeconfig.yaml

If nothing matches (common), it means the UI record is stored in the NAI API DB but the K8s Model CR is already gone.

2) Check for any model-job failures for Llama-3.3

kubectl -n nai-admin get jobs | grep -i model-job
kubectl -n nai-admin get pods | grep -i model-job

3) Delete the Unavailable instance

If it has no active Model CR / job, the cleanest fix is simply:

delete that model instance from the UI (if UI offers delete)
or

delete by backend API (we can do that too, but UI delete is simplest)

If you want CLI-only deletion and the Model CR exists:

kubectl -n nai-admin delete pvc <matching-pvc>   # only if you want to free space

Because it’s the only one whose HF import didn’t complete successfully. Your GPU stack is now healthy, but HF downloads can still fail due to CAS/XET and/or TLS trust inside the model processor container (which we were mid-way addressing earlier).

does not expose Swagger/OpenAPI

there is no supported direct REST cleanup API

Kubernetes CRDs are the source of truth

2) Check the InferenceService status + conditions (fastest truth)

kubectl -n nai-admin describe inferenceservice <ISVC>
kubectl -n nai-admin get inferenceservice <ISVC> -o yaml | egrep -i "conditions:|reason:|message:|url:|traffic:|model|storage|runtime|predictor" -n | head -n 200

You’re looking for Ready=False and a reason like:

RevisionFailed

PredictorConfigurationFailed

RouteNotReady

ModelLoadFailed

FailedMount

ImagePullBackOff

3) Find the predictor pod(s) for that endpoint

kubectl -n nai-admin get pods -o wide | egrep -i "<ISVC>|predictor|kserve" 

Then describe the predictor pod:

kubectl -n nai-admin describe pod <POD_NAME> | tail -n 80

And logs:

kubectl -n nai-admin logs <POD_NAME> --all-containers --tail=200

Common failures show up here immediately:

image pull / auth / TLS

missing model files / storage URI

GPU not available

runtime (vLLM/TGI/NIM) crash

4) Check if it’s a GPU scheduling failure (very common)

kubectl -n nai-admin describe pod <POD_NAME> | egrep -i "Insufficient|nvidia.com/gpu|FailedScheduling|taint|toleration" -n
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"  gpu="}{.status.allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu}{"  used="}{.status.capacity.nvidia\.com/gpu}{"\n"}{end}' | grep gpu || true

If you see Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu, the endpoint will never become ready until a GPU frees up or you reduce GPU requests.

5) Check the service/route/ingress path (endpoint URL failing)

KServe typically creates services/routes. Check:

kubectl -n nai-admin get svc | egrep -i "<ISVC>|predictor|kserve|knative" 
kubectl -n nai-admin get ingress | egrep -i "<ISVC>|kserve|knative|istio" || true

Also check if Knative is used:

kubectl get pods -n knative-serving 2>/dev/null | head
kubectl get pods -n istio-system 2>/dev/null | head
kubectl get pods -n kserve 2>/dev/null | head

6) Quick “why is it failing” event sweep (super useful)

kubectl -n nai-admin get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 40
kubectl -n nai-admin get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | egrep -i "<ISVC>|predictor|kserve|knative|istio|pull|mount|gpu|failed" | tail -n 60

Most common fixes (based on what we’ve seen in your environment)

A) ImagePullBackOff

Usually registry auth/TLS on nodes. The describe pod will show the exact registry and error.

B) GPU not schedulable

Increase available GPUs, reduce endpoint GPU requests, or add tolerations/selector.

C) Model not found / storage mount

PVC not bound, wrong Storage URI, or permission issues.

D) Route/Ingress loop / 404/500

Istio/Knative route not ready; check services + controller pods.

## Response:
1/31/2026, 7:10:23 PM

Yes 👍 — you can cleanly remove the old NVIDIA NGC Personal Key from CLI, even if the UI won’t let you delete it. The UI blocks deletion because it’s still referenced by endpoints or imagePullSecrets.

Below is the safe, correct CLI procedure we use in NAI/NKP environments.

What the NGC key maps to (important)

In NAI, one NGC Personal Key creates two secrets:

NGC API key secret
Used as env var:
NGC_API_KEY

NGC image pull secret
Used to pull from nvcr.io:
kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson

Your old key is:

nai-f4149a92-a691-42d9-b502-8c
nai-f4149a92-a691-42d9-b502-8c-ngc-image-pull

Step 0 — Verify the new key is already working

Before deleting anything, confirm the new NVIDIA key exists:

kubectl -n nai-admin get secret | grep -i ngc

You should see two secrets for the new key as well.

Step 1 — Find what is still referencing the OLD key

This is why UI won’t delete it.

1.1 Find InferenceServices using the old key

kubectl -n nai-admin get inferenceservices -o yaml | \
grep -n "nai-f4149a92-a691-42d9-b502-8c" -n

If you see output → that endpoint must be updated first.

1.2 Find pods still referencing it

kubectl -n nai-admin get pods -o yaml | \
grep -n "nai-f4149a92-a691-42d9-b502-8c" -n

1.3 Find any lingering imagePullSecrets

kubectl -n nai-admin get deploy -o yaml | \
grep -n "nai-f4149a92-a691-42d9-b502-8c-ngc-image-pull"

Step 2 — Patch endpoints to use the NEW NGC key

For each InferenceService that still uses the old key, update it.

Example (replace with your new secret name):

kubectl -n nai-admin patch inferenceservice nvidia-8b-listed --type='json' -p='[
  {
    "op":"replace",
    "path":"/spec/predictor/imagePullSecrets/0/name",
    "value":"<NEW-NGC-IMAGE-PULL-SECRET>"
  },
  {
    "op":"replace",
    "path":"/spec/predictor/containers/0/env/3/valueFrom/secretKeyRef/name",
    "value":"<NEW-NGC-API-SECRET>"
  }
]'

Then restart pods:

kubectl -n nai-admin delete pod -l endpoint=nvidia-8b-listed

Repeat for any other endpoint found in Step 1.

Step 3 — Verify old key is no longer referenced

This must return nothing:

kubectl -n nai-admin get inferenceservices -o yaml | \
grep -n "nai-f4149a92-a691-42d9-b502-8c" || echo "✅ Not referenced"

kubectl -n nai-admin get pods -o yaml | \
grep -n "nai-f4149a92-a691-42d9-b502-8c" || echo "✅ Not referenced"

Step 4 — Delete the old NGC secrets (CLI)

Now the UI restriction is gone, and CLI delete will work.

kubectl -n nai-admin delete secret nai-f4149a92-a691-42d9-b502-8c-ngc-image-pull
kubectl -n nai-admin delete secret nai-f4149a92-a691-42d9-b502-8c

Expected output:

secret "...-ngc-image-pull" deleted
secret "..." deleted

Step 5 — (Optional) Restart NAI API to refresh UI cache

Sometimes the UI caches deleted credentials.

kubectl -n nai-system rollout restart deploy/nai-api
kubectl -n nai-system rollout restart deploy/nai-ui

Why the UI couldn’t delete it (root cause)

NAI protects credentials while referenced

CLI gives you full graph control

This is expected behavior, not a bug

✅ Summary

Yes, CLI is the correct way

You must remove references first

Then delete both secrets

UI will reflect deletion after nai-api restart

If you want, next we can:

Standardize NGC key naming

Switch all NIM models to Harbor-mirrored images

Create a runbook so this never blocks you again

  --docker-email=none@example.com \

]'

If the env index isn’t 3 on your object, use this safer patch method instead (no index dependency):

Explaining secret UI issue and next steps

It seems the UI might show a cached entry, possibly with a new key, but under the same name. I'll provide steps to list secrets, check key timestamps, and ensure the deletion process is complete. Thought for 13s

Got it - and you’re right to be suspicious.

Even though we deleted the old secrets (nai-f414... + ...-ngc-image-pull) and restarted nai-ui, the UI can still show an NGC key entry if:

There is another Kubernetes Secret still holding an NGC key (most likely), or

The UI is reading it from the backend and you need to restart nai-api as well (cache), or

It’s a new key with the same name “NAI” (UI masks the value, so it can look “old”).

Let’s prove which it is - purely from CLI.

1) Find ALL secrets in nai-admin that contain NGC_API_KEY

This is the authoritative check.

Run:

kubectl -n nai-admin get secret -o name | while read s; do
  has_key="$(kubectl -n nai-admin get "$s" -o jsonpath='{.data.NGC_API_KEY}' 2>/dev/null || true)"
  if [ -n "$has_key" ]; then
    echo "$s"
    kubectl -n nai-admin get "$s" -o jsonpath='  created={.metadata.creationTimestamp}{"\n"}'
  fi
done

This will list the secret name(s) and creation time for every stored NGC key.

If it prints one secret and it’s recent → that’s your new key (UI is correct).

If it prints an older secret → that’s the “old key” still present (we can delete it).

If it prints nothing → UI is showing stale state → we restart nai-api.

2) If secrets exist: delete the old one(s)

Once you see the secret name(s), delete the one you don’t want:

kubectl -n nai-admin delete secret <secret-name>

(We already deleted nai-f414..., so it will be a different one.)

Then restart UI/API:

kubectl -n nai-system rollout restart deploy/nai-api
kubectl -n nai-system rollout restart deploy/nai-ui
kubectl -n nai-system rollout status deploy/nai-api
kubectl -n nai-system rollout status deploy/nai-ui

3) If no secrets contain NGC_API_KEY: restart nai-api (not just nai-ui)

You only restarted nai-ui earlier. The UI list is usually served by nai-api.

Do:

kubectl -n nai-system rollout restart deploy/nai-api
kubectl -n nai-system rollout status deploy/nai-api

Then hard refresh the browser.

One more important point

Your UI shows:

Key Name: NAI

If you created the new key with the same name, the UI will still show “NAI” and the masked value will look similar. That doesn’t mean it’s old.

So the CLI check above is the truth.

Paste the output of Step 1

Run the “find ALL secrets with NGC_API_KEY” command and paste the results. I’ll tell you exactly which secret to delete (or confirm it’s just the new one + cache).

Check if NGC key secret exists in nai-system

Run this:

kubectl -n nai-system get secret -o name | while read s; do

    echo "$s"
    kubectl -n nai-system get "$s" -o jsonpath='  created={.metadata.creationTimestamp}{"\n"}'
  fi
done

If it prints a secret → that’s what the UI is showing; we can delete it (after confirming it’s not needed).

If it prints nothing → UI is purely caching/DB and should clear after the nai-api restart + relogin.

## Response:
1/31/2026, 7:34:58 PM

That UI message (“Error in kubernetes operation”) almost always means: NAI UI (via nai-api) tried to create/update a Kubernetes Secret and the Kubernetes API rejected it (RBAC/validation/quota/webhook/etc.).

Let’s get the exact reason from the cluster - it’ll be in nai-api logs or in events.

1) Check nai-api logs for the real error (most direct)

Run this right after reproducing the UI error (or now - it should still show recent failures):

kubectl -n nai-system logs deploy/nai-api --since=30m | egrep -i "kubernetes|secret|forbidden|denied|webhook|quota|invalid|error" | tail -n 80

If that’s too noisy, do last 200 lines:

kubectl -n nai-system logs deploy/nai-api --tail=200

2) Check Kubernetes events in nai-admin (where the secret is usually created)

kubectl -n nai-admin get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 50

3) Quick RBAC sanity: can you create a secret in nai-admin?

This tells us if it’s a permissions policy issue vs an app bug.

kubectl -n nai-admin auth can-i create secrets
kubectl -n nai-admin auth can-i patch secrets

If no → the UI/app also can’t; we need RBAC fix.

If yes → likely the nai-api serviceaccount is missing permissions, or a webhook blocks it.

4) Check what serviceaccount nai-api is running as (then we verify its RBAC)

kubectl -n nai-system get deploy nai-api -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName}{"\n"}'

Then check if that SA can create secrets in nai-admin:

SA="$(kubectl -n nai-system get deploy nai-api -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName}')"
kubectl auth can-i create secrets -n nai-admin --as=system:serviceaccount:nai-system:$SA
kubectl auth can-i patch secrets  -n nai-admin --as=system:serviceaccount:nai-system:$SA

Fast workaround if you need to move NOW

If the UI can’t save the key, you can create the secrets manually in nai-admin and then reference them in your InferenceService.

Example (replace <NEWKEY>):

kubectl -n nai-admin create secret generic nai-ngc-key \
  --from-literal=NGC_API_KEY='<NEWKEY>' \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

kubectl -n nai-admin create secret docker-registry nai-ngc-pull \
  --docker-server=nvcr.io \
  --docker-username='$oauthtoken' \
  --docker-password='<NEWKEY>' \
  --docker-email=none@example.com \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

(Then patch your InferenceService to use nai-ngc-key and nai-ngc-pull.)

Send me these two outputs and I’ll tell you the exact fix

kubectl -n nai-system logs deploy/nai-api --since=30m | egrep -i "secret|forbidden|denied|webhook|quota|invalid|error" | tail -n 80

kubectl -n nai-admin auth can-i create secrets

Once we see the real error (RBAC vs webhook vs invalid secret payload), we’ll apply the smallest correct fix.

Yes - you can test from a GPU node, but don’t run the full skopeo copy on the node yet. First do a lightweight reachability test (fast, no huge downloads). If the node can reach nvcr.io/layers.nvcr.io reliably, then doing the copy there may succeed.

1) Pick one GPU node and SSH

2) Check DNS + TCP connectivity to nvcr + layers

Run on the node:

# DNS + quick HTTPS handshake test (no auth)
getent hosts nvcr.io
getent hosts layers.nvcr.io

# TCP reachability
timeout 5 bash -lc '</dev/tcp/nvcr.io/443' && echo "nvcr.io:443 OK" || echo "nvcr.io:443 FAIL"
timeout 5 bash -lc '</dev/tcp/layers.nvcr.io/443' && echo "layers.nvcr.io:443 OK" || echo "layers.nvcr.io:443 FAIL"

# quick TLS check (shows issuer, proves handshake)
echo | openssl s_client -connect nvcr.io:443 -servername nvcr.io 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer | head -n 1
echo | openssl s_client -connect layers.nvcr.io:443 -servername layers.nvcr.io 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer | head -n 1

If layers.nvcr.io fails or is slow, the full download will keep timing out no matter where you run it.

3) Check if skopeo exists on the node

command -v skopeo || echo "skopeo not installed"

If it says not installed, don’t install packages on nodes unless customer allows. Better to run skopeo from bastion or a separate internet VM.

4) If skopeo IS installed and reachability looks good

Then yes, you can run your retry command on that node. But don’t expose the Harbor password and don’t store the NGC key in shell history.

Use read -s and then run the command exactly as you wrote.

nvcr.io:443 ✅ reachable

layers.nvcr.io:443 ❌ not reachable within 5 seconds (and openssl hung)

Also:

skopeo isn’t installed on nodes (good - we shouldn’t install extra tooling there).

What you can do now (real options)

Option 1 (best): Get the network team to allow layers.nvcr.io:443

You need outbound HTTPS to:

nvcr.io

layers.nvcr.io  (required for blobs)

(sometimes) api.ngc.nvidia.com

Ask them to allowlist:

layers.nvcr.io TCP/443 (and its resolved IP ranges will change; domain-based allowlist is best)

Once it’s reachable, your same skopeo copy command from bastion will work.

Option 2 (best workaround): Download elsewhere, then transfer to bastion

Use any machine that has unrestricted internet to download the image into a tar, then copy it to bastion and push to Harbor.

This avoids your network entirely for the large blob transfer.

On an internet machine:

skopeo copy --all \
  --src-creds '$oauthtoken:<NGC_KEY>' \
  docker://nvcr.io/nim/meta/llama3-8b-instruct:1.0.3 \

Copy tar to bastion, then on bastion:

skopeo copy --all \
  docker-archive:/data/llama3-8b-instruct_1.0.3.tar \
  --dest-tls-verify=false --dest-creds nutanix:'Nutanix/4u' \
  docker://10.156.76.35:5000/nai/nim/meta/llama3-8b-instruct:1.0.3

Option 3 (recommended architecture): Mirror NIM images centrally

If your company has a central egress-enabled staging box, mirror required nvcr.io/nim/... images there into Harbor and keep workload clusters airgapped.

Meanwhile: what you can still run today

Any endpoint that uses images already in Harbor (vLLM / TGI / HF-manual) will work fine. NIM endpoints won’t until layers.nvcr.io is reachable or you import images offline.

Quick one-liner to give the network team (copy-paste)

We can connect to nvcr.io:443 but not to layers.nvcr.io:443 (TCP timeout). NGC container pulls require access to layers.nvcr.io for blob downloads. Please allowlist layers.nvcr.io on TCP/443 (domain-based).

Good question — this confusion is very common, and you’re right to stop and ask 👍
Let’s clear it up cleanly.

Short answer (TL;DR)

nvcr.io/nim/meta/llama3-8b-instruct:1.0.3 is NOT the model itself.
It is a NVIDIA NIM runtime container that serves the model.

Think of it as:

Model = weights
NIM image = engine + server + optimizations to run the model

What this image actually is

nvcr.io/nim/meta/llama3-8b-instruct:1.0.3

This is a NVIDIA NIM (NVIDIA Inference Microservice) container image.

It contains:

A prebuilt inference server

NVIDIA-optimized runtime (TensorRT / Triton stack internally)

Model-specific launch logic

API server (OpenAI-compatible REST endpoints)

GPU optimizations for H100 / A100 / L40 etc.

It does NOT contain the model weights baked inside in the usual sense.

How NIM works (important)

When you deploy a NIM-based endpoint:

Kubernetes pulls the NIM image
(nvcr.io/nim/meta/llama3-8b-instruct:1.0.3)

At startup, the container:
Uses NGC_API_KEY

Downloads model artifacts from NVIDIA NGC

Caches them under:
/mnt/models

Then it exposes an inference API on port 8000

So:

Component
Comes from where
Runtime / server
NIM container image
Model weights
Downloaded dynamically from NGC
GPU optimization
Built into NIM
API
Inside the container

Why this image is failing in your environment

Your logs already proved it:

layers.nvcr.io:443 FAIL

NIM images:

Pull container metadata from nvcr.io

Pull large blobs & model layers from layers.nvcr.io

Since layers.nvcr.io is blocked:

Image pull partially works

Blob download fails

Pod stays in ImagePullBackOff

That’s not an NAI bug — it’s network.

Compare with Hugging Face models (why those work)

HF-based models (working in your cluster)

Example:

meta-llama/Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct

Flow:

NAI job downloads weights from Hugging Face

Stores them in PVC

Uses vLLM / TGI image from Harbor

No external runtime dependency at inference time

✅ Works fine in air-gapped / restricted env

Compare with NIM models (your failing ones)

NIM-based models

Example:

Llama-3.3-70B (NVIDIA NIM)
llama3-8b-instruct (NVIDIA NIM)

Flow:

Pod must pull NIM runtime image from nvcr.io

Must reach layers.nvcr.io

Must authenticate via NGC API key

Downloads runtime + model artifacts at start

❌ Breaks if any of these are blocked

So… what is this image used for?

This image is used only when:

You select Import Mode = NVIDIA NIM

You create an endpoint backed by NIM runtime

You want:
Faster startup

NVIDIA-validated performance

Managed runtime

OpenAI-compatible API out of the box

When you should NOT use it

Do NOT use NIM images when:

Environment is air-gapped

layers.nvcr.io is blocked

You want full offline control

You already have HF weights locally

In those cases:

Use Hugging Face import

Use vLLM / TGI

Run fully from Harbor + PVC

Great diagnostics. Two key findings:

Your probe changes did NOT apply to the running pod. It still shows:

Readiness tcp-socket :8000 delay=0s timeout=1s ...
and no Startup probe at all.

The container is still stuck at:

Preparing model workspace. This step might download additional files...
and port 8000 never opens → readiness keeps failing.

Also, kubelet is still warning about the deleted NGC pull secret:

FailedToRetrieveImagePullSecret (nai-f414...-ngc-image-pull)

So we need to force the Deployment (not only the InferenceService) to pick up:

Harbor pull secret only

remove NGC_API_KEY env

relax readiness / add startup probe

and (important) stop “workspace download” behavior by using a local cache location that exists and is writable, without any NGC dependency.

Right now the container is still trying to use NGC profile logic even though the image is local - that’s expected; NIM may still want to prepare workspace. But in your network, it can’t reach layers.nvcr.io, so it will hang.

The real fix: run NIM in “offline/local” mode

For NIM containers, to avoid NGC downloads you must ensure the model workspace/artifacts are already present and set the correct env so it doesn’t attempt NGC fetch.

In your case, you mounted:

STORAGE_URI = pvc://.../model-files
but inside the pod it shows:

STORAGE_URI: /mnt/models (kserve rewrites to mount path)

Yet NIM is still saying “might download additional files” - meaning the required workspace isn’t present in that PVC path for this NIM runtime.

So we have 2 possible states:

A) You intended this PVC to hold NIM workspace but it’s empty → NIM tries to download → stuck.
B) You don’t need PVC at all, and NIM should run with internal assets → but it still tries to fetch profile assets from NGC.

Fastest reliable approach: run NIM endpoint without STORAGE_URI/PVC, and use Harbor image only, and add long startupProbe so it can initialize. If it still hangs, then this NIM runtime requires pulling additional artifacts online and cannot run fully offline unless you pre-stage those artifacts.

Let’s test the fast approach first.

Step 1 - Recreate endpoint cleanly (no PVC, no NGC secrets)

This avoids all stale references. It’s quicker than fighting the reconciler.

kubectl -n nai-admin delete inferenceservice llama3-8-listed

Considering how the model accesses cached assets and API keys

I’m thinking about how to manage the model’s storage and access to cached assets. If the PVC is populated, the model might not need to fetch new files, but I'll need to check if it has access to the required API key. It seems like the key is still necessary to fetch from local registries, even if there's a failure later.

Thought for 18s

Yep - the logs give a 100% definitive cause:

NIM is failing because it still requires an NGC API key at runtime (for the “NGC hub / profile workspace” fetch), and in your new endpoint you removed NGC_API_KEY.

That’s why it crashes immediately:

Exception: The requested operation requires an API key, but none was found

So even though the container image is now local in Harbor, the NIM runtime still wants NGC_API_KEY to prepare its workspace/profile artifacts.

Fix: Add NGC_API_KEY back (but keep Harbor image)

We will:

Create a new secret in nai-admin with your new NGC key

Patch the InferenceService to include NGC_API_KEY env var from that secret

Restart the pod

⚠️ Don’t paste the key here again. Enter it only in the terminal.

1) Create a new NGC API key secret (nai-admin)

read -s -p "Enter NEW NGC API key: " NGC_NEW; echo

kubectl -n nai-admin delete secret nai-ngc-api --ignore-not-found
kubectl -n nai-admin create secret generic nai-ngc-api \
  --from-literal=NGC_API_KEY="$NGC_NEW"

Verify:

kubectl -n nai-admin get secret nai-ngc-api

2) Patch the InferenceService env list to include NGC_API_KEY

This replaces the env list safely (no index guessing):

kubectl -n nai-admin patch inferenceservice llama3-8-listed --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/predictor/containers/0/env","value":[
    {"name":"NIM_SERVED_MODEL_NAME","value":"llama3-8-listed"},
    {"name":"NGC_API_KEY","valueFrom":{"secretKeyRef":{"name":"nai-ngc-api","key":"NGC_API_KEY"}}}
  ]}
]'

(We keep it minimal; we can add STORAGE/PVC later if needed.)

3) Restart the endpoint pod

kubectl -n nai-admin delete pod -l endpoint=llama3-8-listed
kubectl -n nai-admin get pods -l endpoint=llama3-8-listed -w

4) If it still fails (next likely issue)

Then it will fail with network (because it will try to fetch files from NGC hub and your cluster can’t reach layers.nvcr.io). If that happens, the logs will show timeouts/connection errors instead of “API key missing”.

So after restart, immediately check logs:

POD=$(kubectl -n nai-admin get pods -l endpoint=llama3-8-listed -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl -n nai-admin logs "$POD" -c kserve-container --tail=200

Important reality check

Adding NGC_API_KEY fixes the crash.
But if NIM still needs to download additional artifacts at startup and layers.nvcr.io is blocked, the endpoint may still not reach Ready until you either:

allow outbound to layers.nvcr.io:443, or

pre-stage the required NIM workspace/artifacts offline (more involved)

We’ll know which one it is from the new logs.

Do steps 1-3 now, then paste:

kubectl -n nai-admin logs "$POD" -c kserve-container --tail=60

What the logs prove (root cause)

Your pod is failing inside the NIM container while “Preparing model workspace”, and the hard failure is:

HTTP status client error (402 Payment Required) for url (https://api.ngc.nvidia.com/v2/org/nim/team/meta/models/llama3-8b-instruct/hf/files)
and then it exits with code 1.

So this is NOT a Harbor image issue anymore (you already pulled the image from Harbor successfully).
It is NIM trying to download model artifacts from NGC (xfiles.ngc.nvidia.com / api.ngc.nvidia.com) and your key/org entitlement is not allowed (402).

Also: your pod has NO /mnt/models PVC mounted (volumeMounts only shows /dev/shm and SA token), so even if entitlement was OK, you’re not giving NIM its cache/model workspace mount.

1) Immediate actions to make it work

A) Fix the missing PVC mount (/mnt/models)

Right now, you have no PVC mount. Apply this patch:

kubectl -n nai-admin patch inferenceservice llama3-8-listed --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/predictor/volumes/-","value":{
    "name":"kserve-pvc-source",

  }},
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/predictor/containers/0/volumeMounts/-","value":{
    "name":"kserve-pvc-source",
    "mountPath":"/mnt/models",
    "subPath":"model-files"
  }}
]'

B) Ensure env is complete for NIM

You already have NGC_API_KEY in the InferenceService (good). Add cache vars (safe):

This will fix the missing mount problem, but it will NOT solve the 402 Payment Required (entitlement) problem by itself.

2) What the 402 Payment Required means (plain English)

The key you’re using is valid (it can pull some containers like k8s-driver-manager), but for this NIM model package NVIDIA is returning 402 from the NGC API, meaning:

Your NGC org/user does not have entitlement to download that model artifact bundle via NGC Hub, or

The org/project/team mapping (“org/nim/team/meta/...”) is not permitted with that key.

So you must get a key/org with the right entitlement, or you must run a deployment mode that does not require NGC downloads (fully offline with all artifacts mirrored, if supported by that NIM).

For NIM model runtime + model artifact downloads, safest allowlist is:

nvcr.io TCP 443

layers.nvcr.io TCP 443

api.ngc.nvidia.com TCP 443

xfiles.ngc.nvidia.com TCP 443

So yes, *.nvcr.io is fine, but it is not enough by itself for NIM model artifacts - you also need *.ngc.nvidia.com (at least the two above).

## Response:
2/1/2026, 1:57:33 PM

That warning is expected in NAI when the model/runtime combination isn’t in Nutanix’s “validated matrix” for your exact platform/profile - it’s a support/quality disclaimer, not necessarily a failure.

In your case, you’re running an NVIDIA NIM container (example: nim/meta/llama3-8b-instruct:1.0.3) on GPU passthrough (H100 NVL) with KServe RawDeployment. If Nutanix hasn’t officially validated that specific NIM image version + GPU type + NAI version, the UI shows this banner.

What it means (practically)

The endpoint can still work (and yours is working: health 200 + server started).

Nutanix Support may ask you to reproduce on a validated image/model/version if you open a case.

Performance may vary because the tuned profile (tp/precision/engine) may not match their tested baseline.

How to decide if you can ignore it

If all three are true, you can usually proceed:

Pod is Ready=True

/v1/health/live returns 200

A simple /v1/chat/completions returns a valid response (not 404/500)

Quick “evidence test” you can run (and share)

Run from bastion (inside cluster):

    | head -c 500; echo
  '

If you want to remove the warning

You generally can’t “turn it off”. It goes away only when you deploy something that NAI marks validated (usually:

a model from the NAI catalog that matches your platform, or

a NIM runtime/version that Nutanix explicitly supports for your NAI version + GPU type)

Root cause

So the correct way to reach the service is port 80, not 8000.

That’s why this timed out:

Because 10.106.3.237:8000 is not a listening service port.

All 4 returning HTTP=401 means one of these is true (most likely #1 or #2):

The gateway is not expecting those headers (it expects a different header name), OR

The key you used is not the EnterpriseAI gateway key (it’s an NGC/NIM key, or some other credential), OR

The gateway expects an API key + something else (cookie/session/CSRF, or different auth flow), OR

The request is not reaching the right component (but your earlier response explicitly said “API key is not provided”, so it is reaching the gateway/auth layer).

Let’s prove which one in 2 minutes.

1) Get the real error body (very important)

Run ONE of these with a fake key so we see the exact message:

curl -k -s \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer FAKE" \
  -d '{"model":"meta/llama3-8b-instruct","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello"}],"max_tokens":16}' \
  "https://10.156.77.36/enterpriseai/v1/chat/completions"

If it still says “API key is not provided”, then that header is ignored by the gateway.

If it changes to “invalid api key / unauthorized”, then the header name is correct but key is wrong.

Do the same for x-api-key (FAKE):

curl -k -s \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-api-key: FAKE" \
  -d '{"model":"meta/llama3-8b-instruct","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello"}],"max_tokens":16}' \
  "https://10.156.77.36/enterpriseai/v1/chat/completions"

2) Find which header the gateway expects (from the cluster)

Because this is NAI/EnterpriseAI, the expected header is usually configured in an Envoy Gateway / AI Gateway / extproc config.

Try these searches in the NAI cluster (this is safe and fast):

# search for "api key" and auth header hints
kubectl -n nai-system get cm,secret,deploy,sts -o yaml | egrep -i "api[-_ ]key|x-api-key|authorization|bearer|apikey|header" | head -n 200

Also search anything enterpriseai / gateway / extproc:

kubectl -A get deploy,sts,cm,secret -o yaml | egrep -i "enterpriseai|ai-gateway|extproc|envoy|ratelimit|auth" | head -n 200

We’re looking for a line like:

apiKeyHeaderName: ...

header: x-api-key

AuthorizationHeader: ...

API_KEY_HEADER=...

ENTERPRISEAI_API_KEY_HEADER=...

3) Confirm you’re using the correct key type

The key you need for https://10.156.77.36/enterpriseai/... is NOT an NGC “nvapi-...” key.

It should be an EnterpriseAI / NAI API Gateway key (often created in the UI under API Keys / Access Tokens / Gateway keys depending on version). If you only have nvapi- keys, those are for nvcr.io / NIM / NGC, not for EnterpriseAI gateway.

4) Extra quick check: see if 401 is coming from Envoy (gateway) vs app

Run:

curl -k -s -D- -o /dev/null \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"meta/llama3-8b-instruct","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello"}],"max_tokens":16}' \
  "https://10.156.77.36/enterpriseai/v1/chat/completions" | head -n 40

If you see headers like server: envoy or x-envoy-*, that confirms the gateway is rejecting the auth before it reaches the model.

The gateway expects x-api-key

Thought for 34s

Good - now we proved the header is definitely leaving curl, but the gateway at 10.156.77.36 still says “API key is not provided”. That almost always means one of these two things:

Below is the fastest way to prove which one it is, using only CLI.

Step 5 - About your API key value (important)

That value c0d4c493-... looks like a UUID. Many platforms show keys as:

A real secret value (often long, sometimes prefixed like nai_...), OR

A credential object ID (UUID) that is not the actual key.

If the gateway expects the real secret and you send a UUID, sometimes it still says “not provided” (or “invalid”), depending on implementation.

• Your current key is unknown to nai-api

Where the Inference API key comes from

Option 1 (Recommended): NAI UI

This is the normal and supported way.

Path:

NAI UI → API Keys → Create API Key → Inference

Exact flow

Go to API Keys

Click Create API Key

✅ meta/llama3-8b-instruct

Option 2 (CLI / backend – only if UI not accessible)

kubectl -n nai-system exec deploy/nai-api -- \

Or inspect DB mappings (advanced, not recommended unless UI broken).

What NOT to use (common confusion)

Do NOT use these for inference API:

Key type
Why it fails
NGC / nvapi key
Only for pulling models
Harbor credentials
Registry only
Random UUID
Not registered in nai-api
x-api-key header
❌ Not used by NAI
Plain token without Bearer
❌ Middleware rejects it

Correct request format (final)

Once you have the Inference API key from NAI UI:

curl -k \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <INFERENCE_API_KEY>" \

    "messages": [{"role":"user","content":"Say hello"}],

What you do need to be careful about is which token you are changing:

1) If you are changing the “Inference API Key” (the one used by clients)

You do not need to recreate the endpoint.

You only need to create a new Inference API Key in UI and use it in curl:

Endpoint stays the same

Model stays the same

Only the client header changes

This is the cleanest.

If your curl still returns 401 missing bearer api key or failed to validate API Key against endpoint, it usually means:

The request is not reaching the right auth route, OR

The key is not bound to the correct endpoint in UI, OR

You’re sending it in the wrong header format

NAI expects:
Authorization: Bearer <inference-api-key>
Not x-api-key.

2) If you are changing the “NGC API Key” (nvapi… used by NIM to download extra files)

Then yes - endpoint pods may need restart/redeploy because the container reads NGC key as env.

But in your final working setup, you solved this by serving the NIM image from Harbor.
Even then, the NIM container can still try to hit NGC (“Preparing model workspace…”) so keeping a valid NGC key is still helpful.

However, changing NGC key does not require recreating endpoint. You can:

Update the Kubernetes secret used by the endpoint

Restart the predictor pods

3) If UI won’t let you “update” an API key

That’s expected in many systems: keys are immutable. You usually:

Create a new key

Switch clients to use it

Revoke/delete old key (if supported)

So the correct process is rotate, not “edit”.

import re, pathlib
import openai_harmony as oh

urls = sorted(set(re.findall(r'https?://[^\"\\s\\)]+', t)))

print('---- urls found ----')

If that still prints NO_URLS_FOUND, run this next (it searches the whole installed module directory for URLs):

kubectl -n nai-admin exec -it gpt20b-debug -- sh -lc "python3 - <<'PY'
import re, pathlib, openai_harmony as oh

root = pathlib.Path(oh.__file__).resolve().parent
hits = []

for f in root.rglob('*.py'):
    try:
        txt = f.read_text(errors='ignore')
    except Exception:
        continue
    for u in re.findall(r'https?://[^\"\\s\\)]+', txt):
        hits.append((str(f), u))

print('openai_harmony dir:', root)
print('---- url hits ----')
if not hits:
    print('NO_URLS_FOUND')
else:
    for f,u in sorted(set(hits)):
        print(f'{f}  ->  {u}')
PY"

Paste the output you get (the URL(s) or “NO_URLS_FOUND”), and I’ll tell you the next step.

class StreamableParser:
    """Incremental parser over completion tokens."""

def __init__(self, encoding: HarmonyEncoding, role: Role | None):
    role_str = str(role.value) if role is not None else None
    self._inner = _PyStreamableParser(encoding._inner, role_str)

def process(self, token: int) -> "StreamableParser":
    self._inner.process(token)
    return self

@property
def current_content(self) -> str:
    return self._inner.current_content

@property
def current_role(self) -> Optional[Role]:
    raw = self._inner.current_role
    return Role(raw) if raw is not None else None

@property
def current_content_type(self) -> Optional[str]:
    return self._inner.current_content_type

@property
def last_content_delta(self) -> Optional[str]:
    return self._inner.last_content_delta

@property
def messages(self) -> List[Message]:
    raw = self._inner.messages
    return [Message.from_dict(m) for m in json.loads(raw)]

@property
def tokens(self) -> List[int]:
    return self._inner.tokens

@property
def state_data(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Return a JSON string representing the parser's internal state."""
    return json.loads(self._inner.state)

@property
def state(self) -> StreamState:
    data = self.state_data
    return StreamState(data["state"])

@property
def current_recipient(self) -> Optional[str]:
    return self._inner.current_recipient

@property
def current_channel(self) -> Optional[str]:
    return self._inner.current_channel

def load_harmony_encoding(name: str | "HarmonyEncodingName") -> HarmonyEncoding:  # type: ignore[name-defined]
    """Load an encoding by name (delegates to the Rust implementation)."""

# Allow both strings and enum values.

    name = str(name)

inner: _PyHarmonyEncoding = _load_harmony_encoding(name)
return HarmonyEncoding(inner)

Why llama3-8b-instruct works but gpt-oss-20b fails

Your Llama NIM endpoint can run from the image you mirrored into Harbor and (once NGC API key is set) it doesn’t require this OpenAI harmony vocab download path.

gpt-oss-20b specifically uses OpenAI Harmony encoding, which downloads vocab files from:
openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net/encodings/...
If that’s blocked, the container starts, loads weights, then crashes right before serving.

Thought for 1m 27s

Yes - the gpt-oss-20b failure is now clearly explained by what you found.

1) What site + port must be open (for gpt-oss-20b NIM)

Your gpt-oss-20b container crashes because openai_harmony tries to download tiktoken encoding files from:

openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net : 443/tcp (Azure Blob)

You already proved it’s blocked from GPU node (curl exit 28 / TCP FAIL). That’s why you see:

openai_harmony.HarmonyError: ... failed to download or load vocab file

and your strings output shows the exact URL:
https://openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net/encodings/... (the encodings are o200k_base.tiktoken, cl100k_base.tiktoken, etc.)

Also note: your DNS resolves it to an Azure storage hostname like:

blob.dm2prdstf01a.store.core.windows.net (still 443/tcp)

So if your firewall allowlisting is strict, the safest allow is:

openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net:443

and optionally *.blob.core.windows.net:443 / *.store.core.windows.net:443 (depends on how your network team does it)

Proof commands (copy-paste for customer)

Run on bastion:

getent hosts openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net
timeout 5 bash -lc '</dev/tcp/openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net/443' && echo "OK" || echo "FAIL"
curl -vk --max-time 15 https://openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net/encodings/o200k_base.tiktoken -o /dev/null

Run on a GPU node (same test):

getent hosts openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net
timeout 5 bash -lc '</dev/tcp/openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net/443' && echo "OK" || echo "FAIL"
curl -vk --max-time 15 https://openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net/encodings/o200k_base.tiktoken -o /dev/null

If it fails, you get exactly what you already captured: connect timeout.

2) Why this happens (short, factual)

tiktoken-rust (used by the Harmony encoding loader) downloads and caches files from Azure Blob, and it honors this env var: TIKTOKEN_CACHE_DIR. (Docs.rs)

So in airgapped / restricted egress, gpt-oss-* will fail unless either:

you allow the outbound HTTPS to that Azure Blob host, or

you pre-seed the cache files in the expected cache dir (offline workaround).

3) What to ask the network team (minimal)

For gpt-oss-* NIM to come up cleanly:

openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net TCP 443

(Separately, for NVIDIA NIM image pulls you already worked through: nvcr.io + layers.nvcr.io TCP 443.)

4) Your internal gateway 401 issue (why your API key didn’t work)

Your gateway (https://10.156.77.36/enterpriseai/v1/chat/completions) is rejecting because it expects a Bearer API key and validates it against the endpoint ID. Your nai-api logs even say: “missing bearer api key” and then “failed to validate API Key against endpoint with ID: meta/llama3-8b-instruct”. (This matches the behavior you saw.)

So:

Use Authorization: Bearer <INFERENCE_KEY_VALUE>

The value must be the real secret key string shown at creation time in UI (not the UUID-looking ID).

And it must be scoped/linked to the endpoint you are calling.

Example format:

curl -k -s \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <PASTE_INFERENCE_KEY_VALUE_HERE>" \
  -d '{"model":"meta/llama3-8b-instruct","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello"}],"max_tokens":16}' \
  "https://10.156.77.36/enterpriseai/v1/chat/completions"

5) Your office chat snippet - yes, it helps

It’s consistent with what we’re seeing:

gpt-oss-* needs a dependency download (the tiktoken encodings).

You can workaround by pre-downloading encodings + setting env vars, but it’s “fragile” unless NAI product supports it cleanly.

Quick answer to your earlier yes/no

Yes, you can stop Terminal 1 if it’s just the port-forward and you’re done with it.

If you want to proceed step-by-step (your preferred mode), send me:

Output of the GPU node test for openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net:443 after network team change (OK/FAIL), and

Whether you want to solve gpt-oss-20b by network allowlist or offline cache seeding.

## Prompt:
2/2/2026, 3:25:12 PM

Patch probes what is this for ?

## Response:
2/2/2026, 3:25:16 PM

Good question 👍
Short answer: it tells Kubernetes to wait long enough while a big model is starting, instead of killing it too early.

Let me explain simply, without commands.

What “patch probes” means

In Kubernetes, every container can have health checks called probes.
They decide when a pod is allowed to live and when traffic can go to it.

For large NIM models like gpt-oss-20b, startup is slow (minutes).

The problem you’re hitting

Right now your pod shows:

Model is loading

vLLM is compiling CUDA graphs

Tokenizer / harmony vocab is being prepared

Port 8000 is NOT open yet

But Kubernetes is doing this:

“I tried port 8000, it’s not open → pod is unhealthy”

So Kubernetes keeps:

Marking it unhealthy

Restarting it

Putting it into CrashLoopBackOff

Even though nothing is actually wrong.

What each probe does (plain English)

1. Startup Probe

Purpose:

“Is the application still starting? Don’t kill it yet.”

For gpt-20b this can be:

2–5 minutes

Sometimes more on first run

Startup probe tells Kubernetes:

“Give me time. Don’t judge me until startup is finished.”

2. Readiness Probe

Purpose:

“Is the service ready to accept traffic?”

Until this is ready = true:

No requests go to the model

UI may say endpoint is active but inference won’t work

We delay readiness because:

Port 8000 opens only after model load finishes

Why this is REQUIRED for gpt-oss-20b

From your logs we clearly see:

Model weights loaded ✔

CUDA graph compile took ~100 seconds ✔

Vocabulary / tokenizer loading happens late ✔

This is expected behavior, not an error.

Without probe tuning:

Kubernetes kills the pod before it finishes

You never reach inference

What patching probes achieves

After patching:

Kubernetes will wait up to ~20 minutes

No restarts during model load

Pod becomes Ready: True only when port 8000 is really listening

Inference starts working normally

Important reassurance

This does NOT modify the model

This does NOT affect performance

This does NOT break future upgrades

This is standard practice for large LLMs

Next step

If you’re okay with this explanation, say “OK, apply probes” and we continue step by step.

If everything is healthy, one of them will go away and you’ll end with exactly 1 running pod.

can you give me a summery a shot one what was the problem with gpt-oss model with details and how did we fix to post in internal office group

## Response:
2/2/2026, 5:21:41 PM

Here’s a short, clean internal summary you can post 👇
(I’ve kept it crisp, technical, and factual)

GPT-OSS-20B deployment issue – Root cause & fix (Summary)

Problem
The gpt-oss-20b NIM endpoint failed to become Ready and kept restarting. Even after the image pulled successfully, the container crashed before opening port 8000, causing readiness probe failures.

Root Causes

Missing external dependency (tiktoken vocab)
The gpt-oss-20b NIM runtime uses openai_harmony which dynamically downloads the tokenizer vocab (o200k_base.tiktoken) from
openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net.
In our environment this domain was initially blocked, causing:

openai_harmony.HarmonyError: error downloading or loading vocab file

Long model initialization time
gpt-oss-20b performs heavy initialization (model load + torch.compile + CUDA graph capture), taking several minutes.
Default readiness/startup probes killed the pod before it could bind to port 8000.

NGC image pull authentication inconsistency
Image pulls intermittently failed due to missing/default imagePullSecrets on the ServiceAccount, even though the secret existed.

Fixes Applied

Network

Allowed outbound HTTPS (TCP 443) to:
openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net

nvcr.io

layers.nvcr.io

Verified access by successfully downloading o200k_base.tiktoken from GPU nodes.

Kubernetes configuration

Patched the InferenceService to relax probes:
Increased startupProbe.failureThreshold

Added initialDelaySeconds to readinessProbe

This allowed the model to fully initialize before health checks.

Image pull reliability

Attached the NGC docker-registry secret to the default ServiceAccount in nai-admin.

Ensured all pods consistently authenticate to nvcr.io.

Replica cleanup

Scaled down the old ReplicaSet created during rolling updates, leaving a single healthy pod.

Result

gpt-oss-20b pod reaches Ready = True

NIM server successfully binds to port 8000

Endpoint works via:
Internal service (/v1/chat/completions)

NAI UI

Model inference confirmed working

Key takeaway
gpt-oss-20b is not fully air-gapped by default. It requires external tokenizer assets unless pre-seeded, and needs longer startup tolerances due to heavy initialization.

If you want, I can also give you:

a 1-liner TL;DR, or

a “Lessons Learned / Best Practices” follow-up for future NIM deployments.

## Response:

Here’s the same content, tightened and with the full model / NVIDIA context added, ready to paste:

Lessons Learned / Best Practices

NVIDIA NIM model nvcr.io/nim/openai/gpt-oss-20b (GPT-OSS-20B) is not fully air-gapped; it requires outbound access to openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net (TCP 443) to download tokenizer (tiktoken / Harmony vocab) files unless they are pre-staged under /mnt/models.

Large NVIDIA NIM models (20B+) require extended startup and readiness probes due to heavy initialization (model shard load, torch.compile, CUDA graph capture).

NGC imagePullSecrets must be attached to the ServiceAccount, not only the pod or InferenceService spec, to prevent intermittent 401 Unauthorized and ImagePullBackOff from nvcr.io / layers.nvcr.io.

Rolling updates create multiple ReplicaSets during patches; old ReplicaSets should be scaled down to avoid duplicate pods and scheduling confusion.

an ultra-short Slack version (2 lines)

or a runbook-style checklist for future GPT-OSS / NIM deployments

## Response:

Diagnosing SSL cert verification issues in pod

It seems like SSL issues might be due to proxy interception or missing corporate certificates inside the container. Check if outbound traffic uses a proxy, and verify SSL certificates in /etc/ssl/certs. Run curl -v https://huggingface.co inside the pod to check the cert chain. If needed, mount the CA secret manually or use specific environment variables like SSL_CERT_FILE or REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE.

Thought for 21s

That error is very clear: the model-processor pod can reach huggingface.co, but the TLS certificate chain is not trusted inside the container:

SSLCertVerificationError: certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate

This almost always means one of these is true:

Your network is doing TLS inspection / proxy, and Hugging Face is presenting a cert signed by an internal/corporate CA that the container does not trust.

Or the container image is missing/old CA bundle (less common).

Next step is to prove which CA is being presented, then we add that CA into the pod trust store.

Run these commands (copy/paste as-is). Replace the pod name if it changes.

POD="nai-0a08fa93-931d-4002-81e5-b1-model-job-dld88"

# 1) Confirm DNS + basic connectivity to Hugging Face from inside the pod
kubectl -n nai-admin exec -it "$POD" -- sh -lc '
getent hosts huggingface.co || true
timeout 5 sh -lc "</dev/tcp/huggingface.co/443" && echo TCP_443_OK || echo TCP_443_FAIL
'

# 2) Show the TLS issuer being presented (this is the key proof)
kubectl -n nai-admin exec -it "$POD" -- sh -lc '
echo | openssl s_client -connect huggingface.co:443 -servername huggingface.co -showcerts 2>/dev/null \
| openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer
'

# 3) Try curl with verbose TLS output (will show the exact verify error)
kubectl -n nai-admin exec -it "$POD" -- sh -lc '
curl -vk --max-time 15 https://huggingface.co/ -o /dev/null 2>&1 | tail -n 40
'

Send me the output of step #2 (subject/issuer) and the last ~40 lines of step #3.

What we’ll do after you paste that:

If the issuer is NOT a public CA (e.g., it looks like your company / proxy), we will:
export that corporate root CA (PEM),

create a Kubernetes secret in nai-admin,

mount it into the model-processor job and set:
SSL_CERT_FILE and/or REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE (Python/requests),

and optionally update the OS trust store if the container supports it.

Temporary workaround (only if you must unblock quickly; not recommended long-term):

# This disables SSL verification for Hugging Face downloads inside that container.
# Use only for testing, then revert.
HF_HUB_DISABLE_SSL_VERIFICATION=1

But the correct fix is to trust the right CA inside the model-processor pod.
